Accountable obligation owner.value: Owns the ERISA participant-complaint queue across every administered Group Health, Group Life, Group Disability, Group Long-Term Care and Retirement / 401(k) plan; escalates fiduciary-breach and participant-data allegations to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee and the Chief Info Security Officer.

Citation verified against current regula.value: Yes — EBSA Cybersecurity Program Best Practices (2021) and Compliance Assistance Release 2021-01 re-read on dol.gov/agencies/ebsa each quarter alongside ERISA §404(e) (29 U.S.C. §1104(e)) service-provider selection duty and the 29 CFR 2560.503-1(h) appeal-rights language quoted in participant responses.

In-scope processes.value: Participant, beneficiary and plan-sponsor complaint intake (contact centre, secure message, DOL/EBSA Benefits Advisor referral, state DOI forward, broker escalation) → ERISA subtype coding → investigation → 30-day substantive response → root-cause analysis → remediation, for every ERISA plan the company administers or recordkeeps.

In-scope systems.value: Complaint cases opened, SLA-timed and dispositioned in the case management tool under ERISA-CLAIMS / ERISA-FEE / ERISA-CYBER / ERISA-SERVICE subtypes, with the recorded call or secure-message thread from Genesys Cloud and, for data-exposure allegations, the SIEM/SOAR incident id linked on the case.

Compliance procedure documented.value: ERISA Participant Complaint Handling & Root Cause Procedure — intake and coding within 1 business day, acknowledgement in 2 business days, substantive response in 30 calendar days, mandatory escalation triggers for fiduciary-breach and unauthorised-access allegations, the 9-code root-cause taxonomy and the remediation-tracking rules.

Compliance procedure approved.value: Approved by the Head of Compliance and ratified by the ERISA Plan Administration Committee; re-approved every 12 months and out-of-cycle whenever EBSA reissues its Cybersecurity Program Best Practices or a new Compliance Assistance Release lands.

Filing/reporting deadlines tracked.value: Continuous: acknowledge in 2 business days, substantive written response in 30 calendar days, state DOI-forwarded complaints answered inside the 10-business-day date on the DOI transmittal, EBSA Benefits Advisor inquiries answered by the date printed on the EBSA letter, and complaints attached to a live claim appeal inherit the 29 CFR 2560.503-1 60-day appeal decision clock.

Deadline reminders configured.value: Case management SLA timers fire to the assigned Complaints Specialist at day 2, day 15 and day 25 and to the Market Conduct / Consumer Compliance Manager at day 28; DOI and EBSA cases carry a hard-stop timer set from the regulator's own due date.

Evidence retained per the retention requ.value: Complaint case file (intake record, call recording, correspondence, investigation notes, root-cause memo, remediation proof) retained 6 years from resolution per ERISA §107 and, where the complaint touches a benefit entitlement, for as long as relevant to that claim per ERISA §209.

Violations/exceptions logged with dispos.value: Missed 30-day responses, complaints mis-coded away from an ERISA subtype, and root causes past their remediation due date are raised as GRC issues with owner, due date, closure evidence and a mandatory retest flag.

Remediation sign-off captured.value: Signs off closure of every ERISA root-cause remediation and personally clears any complaint alleging a fiduciary breach, a fee-disclosure failure or unauthorised access to participant data.

Test population (in-scope transactions,.value: All complaints closed in the quarter carrying an ERISA plan number, plus every DOL/EBSA Benefits Advisor referral and state DOI forward received in the quarter regardless of how it was coded, plus all participant-data incident tickets that generated participant contact.

Pass/fail thresholds.value: At least 98% acknowledged within 2 business days and answered within 30 calendar days; zero tolerance for an EBSA or DOI referral answered after the regulator's date, for an ERISA-CYBER complaint not linked to a SIEM/SOAR incident id, and for a root cause left unremediated past due; SLA breach above 2% escalates to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee.

Compliance test frequency matched to the.value: Obligation is continuous, so monitoring is a monthly SLA and volume dashboard review, a full sample-based test each quarter, and an annual root-cause trend report to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee.

Evidence location for test results.value: Quarterly ERISA complaint test workpaper — population extract with row counts, sample selection with seed, re-performance notes, SLA day-count recomputation, exception schedule — filed in the compliance evidence repository under ERISA / Market Conduct / <quarter>.

Regulator-ready documentation.value: Complaint register in NAIC Market Conduct Annual Statement complaint-record layout with an added ERISA plan number and subtype column, produced with the underlying correspondence packs within 10 business days of an EBSA, DOI or plan-sponsor request.

Regulator response path.value: Market Conduct / Consumer Compliance Manager owns EBSA Benefits Advisor and state DOI responses; General Counsel clears any wording that concedes a fiduciary breach, a prohibited transaction or a reportable participant-data incident before it leaves the building.

checklist.step: Capture every ERISA-touching complaint into one register
actions: Sweep the four intake channels daily: the participant service queue in Genesys Cloud, the secure-message inbox on the Customer Self-Service Portal, the compliance mailbox that receives EBSA Benefits Advisor and state DOI transmittals, and broker escalations from the Broker Relationship Manager.
Open a case in the case management tool for each item and paste the complainant's own words verbatim into the Allegation field — never a paraphrase.
Record channel, receipt date and time, complainant type (participant, beneficiary, alternate payee, plan sponsor, regulator) and whether the contact arrived through a regulator.
Attach the source artifact: the call recording id from Genesys Cloud, the secure-message PDF, or the scanned EBSA/DOI transmittal letter.
Hand any item that is really a benefit claim appeal to the claims appeal queue and cross-link the two case ids so the 29 CFR 2560.503-1 clock is owned by one team.
checklist.done: every item received that day has a case with verbatim allegation text, a receipt timestamp and its source artifact attached.

checklist.step: Code the case to the plan, plan number and ERISA subtype
actions: Look the complainant up in the recordkeeping system and copy the plan name, the three-digit ERISA plan number and the plan sponsor EIN onto the case header.

Set the ERISA subtype: ERISA-CLAIMS (denial, appeal handling, timing), ERISA-FEE (404(a)(5) participant fee disclosure or fund expenses), ERISA-CYBER (unauthorised access, account takeover, phishing, lost data), ERISA-SERVICE (contribution posting, distribution delay, statement error).
Set the plan type flag (Group Health, Group Life, Group Disability, Group Long-Term Care, Retirement / 401(k), Pension Risk Transfer) because it drives the response deadline.
Where the allegation names a recordkeeper, TPA or custodian, tag the service provider from the vendor master so the Third-Party Risk Manager sees it.
Leave the subtype blank rather than guessing, and route to the Consumer Affairs Analyst for a same-day coding call.
checklist.done: the case carries plan name, ERISA plan number, sponsor EIN, subtype and — where alleged — the named service provider.

checklist.step: Acknowledge the complainant and start the response clock
actions: Issue the acknowledgement letter from the approved template within 2 business days, naming the case id, the assigned handler and the 30-calendar-day response date.
Set the SLA timer on the case: day 2 acknowledgement, day 15 status check, day 25 draft-due, day 28 manager alert, day 30 response due.
For a state DOI forward, override the timer with the due date printed on the DOI transmittal (commonly 10 business days) and mark the case Regulator-Driven.
For an EBSA Benefits Advisor referral, override with the date on the EBSA letter and copy the Compliance Manager on the case assignment.
Send the acknowledgement to the address of record from the recordkeeping system, not the address in the complaint, unless an address change has been separately verified.
checklist.done: an acknowledgement is out inside 2 business days and the case shows a due date derived from the correct regulator or internal clock.

checklist.step: Pull the participant's plan record and full claim history
actions: Retrieve the participant's enrolment record, contribution and payroll-remittance history, distribution and loan history, and the last four quarterly benefit statements.

For a claims allegation, ask the Benefits Administrator for the claim file: the initial determination letter, its mail date, the 29 CFR 2560.503-1 day counts applied, the appeal submission and the appeal decision letter.
Pull the participant's notice-delivery history — SPD, SMM, SAR, 404(a)(5) fee disclosure, blackout notice — with the delivery method and date recorded against each.
Confirm from the recordkeeper's audit trail who accessed the participant's account in the 90 days before the complaint, and export that access log to the case.
Write a one-page fact chronology onto the case with a date, an actor and a source document reference on every line.
checklist.done: the case holds a sourced fact chronology plus the claim file, notice-delivery history and 90-day account access log.

checklist.step: Screen the allegation for fiduciary-breach and cyber triggers
actions: Read the verbatim allegation against the escalation trigger list: imprudent selection or monitoring of a service provider (ERISA §404(a)(1)(B)), fees not disclosed, plan assets used for other than participant benefit, denial without the 2560.503-1 notice content, and unauthorised access to or disclosure of participant data.
Where any trigger fires, set case severity to High and notify the ERISA Plan Administration Committee secretary and General Counsel the same business day.
For ERISA-CYBER cases, notify the Chief Info Security Officer and the Incident Response Lead within 4 hours and record the notification time on the case.
Freeze the participant's distribution and address-change privileges through the recordkeeping system while an account-takeover allegation is open.
Record the trigger decision — fired or not fired, and why — on the case so a clean screen is auditable too.
checklist.done: each case shows a dated trigger screen and, where a trigger fired, timestamped notification to Committee, Counsel or the CISO.

checklist.step: Hand participant-data allegations to the security incident process
actions: Open an incident in SIEM/SOAR classified Participant Data — ERISA and paste the complaint case id into the incident reference field so the two records point at each other.

Query authentication and session logs for the participant's account over the 90 days before the complaint: source IPs, device fingerprints, failed MFA challenges, password and email-address changes, and any call-centre-initiated reset.
Determine whether the access was the participant, an authorised delegate, an internal user or an unknown actor, and record the determination with the log evidence attached.

Where an unknown actor is confirmed, invoke the incident response plan required by EBSA Cybersecurity Program Best Practices — contain, notify the plan sponsor as a fiduciary matter, and involve the Privacy Officer on state breach-notification timing.
Return the incident conclusion and its evidence pack to the complaint case within 10 business days of intake.
checklist.done: every ERISA-CYBER case carries a SIEM/SOAR incident id, an access determination and log evidence, returned inside 10 business days.

checklist.step: Test the service-provider angle when a vendor is named
actions: Pull the named provider's file from the vendor master: the ERISA §408(b)(2) fee disclosure, the current contract with its cybersecurity and audit clauses, and the latest SOC 2 Type II report with its bridge letter.
Check whether the complained-of failure sits inside the provider's contracted scope, and identify the contract clause and service level it breached.
Request from the provider a written incident or error account with dates, root cause and corrective action, giving them 10 business days.
Record the provider's response quality and timeliness in the vendor scorecard, because prudent monitoring under ERISA §404(a)(1)(B) is evidenced by this file, not by the contract alone.
Escalate a provider with two or more substantiated complaints in a rolling 12 months to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee for a retention decision.
checklist.done: the vendor file shows the applicable clause, a dated written provider account and a scorecard entry for the complaint.

checklist.step: Write and issue the substantive response inside 30 days
actions: Draft the response against the fact chronology, answering each distinct allegation in its own numbered paragraph — no bundled answers.
Quote the specific plan document or SPD section relied on, with its section number, and enclose the page if the participant has not been sent it.

Where a claim determination is involved, restate the 29 CFR 2560.503-1(g) content — the specific reason, the plan provision relied on, any internal rule or clinical criterion used, and the participant's right to bring a civil action under ERISA §502(a).
State plainly what is being corrected, by when, and what the participant needs do — nothing.

Have the Consumer Affairs Manager review any response that declines the complaint in whole, then send by the participant's elected delivery method and file the sent copy and delivery proof on the case.
checklist.done: a paragraph-by-paragraph response with plan-section citations and §502(a) rights language is sent and proof of delivery is on the case by day 30.

checklist.step: Answer EBSA and state DOI referrals through the regulator channel
actions: Build the regulator response pack: the EBSA or DOI transmittal, the chronology, the plan document and SPD extracts, the notice-delivery history and the participant response already sent.
Answer every numbered question in the regulator's letter in the regulator's own order and numbering.
Route the draft to General Counsel where the answer concedes a late notice, a missed appeal deadline, a fee-disclosure gap or a data incident, and hold the send until counsel clears it in writing.
Send through the channel the regulator specified — the EBSA Benefits Advisor's named contact, or the state DOI complaint portal case thread — and never by ordinary email where a portal exists.
File the submission confirmation, the sent pack and the counsel clearance on the case and on the regulator log.
checklist.done: the regulator's questions are answered in their own numbering, cleared by counsel where required, and submitted with a filed confirmation before their stated date.

checklist.step: Assign a root cause to every closed ERISA case
actions: At closure, code the case to one of the nine taxonomy causes: claim decision error, claim timing miss, notice not delivered, notice content defect, fee disclosure gap, contribution or distribution processing error, recordkeeper data error, access control failure, or communication tone/clarity.
Name the failing control and the process step it sits in, referencing the ERISA plan administration process map rather than a team name.
Distinguish a one-off from a pattern by querying the last 12 months of cases on the same cause, plan and provider, and record the hit count on the case.
Where the same cause has three or more hits in 12 months, mark the case Systemic and open a remediation action — a systemic cause may not be closed as 'coaching delivered'.
Reject any closure coded 'no error found' unless the chronology shows the participant's factual premise was tested and disproved.
checklist.done: every closed case carries a taxonomy cause, a named failing control, a 12-month hit count and a systemic flag where the count warrants it.

checklist.step: Open owned remediation actions for systemic causes
actions: Raise a GRC issue for each systemic cause with the case ids behind it, the failing control, the plans affected and the participant population exposed.
Name a single accountable owner from the process that failed — Benefits Administration, Retirement Operations, the CISO organisation or the recordkeeper relationship — never 'Compliance'.
Set a remediation due date proportionate to exposure: 30 days for access-control and notice-delivery failures, 90 days for process or system changes.
Require the owner to state the closure evidence up front (a reprocessed population, a corrected template, a control test result) so closure cannot be argued later.
Add every open issue to the monthly ERISA remediation report and carry it into next quarter's compliance test as a mandatory retest row.
checklist.done: each systemic cause has a GRC issue with a named process owner, a dated deadline and pre-agreed closure evidence.

checklist.step: Feed cyber root causes into the written security program
actions: Take every ERISA-CYBER root cause into the quarterly control review and map it to the EBSA Cybersecurity Program Best Practices item it failed — access control, encryption, third-party assessment, incident response or business resiliency.

Where the cause is account takeover, review the participant authentication path end to end: portal MFA enrolment rates, call-centre identity proofing script, and self-service email and bank-detail change controls.
Raise the control change through the security change process and record the target control state and the test that will prove it.
Report ERISA-derived cyber findings to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee, not only to the technology risk committee, because the fiduciary duty sits with the plan committee.
Update the participant-facing security guidance on the Customer Self-Service Portal where the cause was participant-side credential compromise.
checklist.done: each ERISA-CYBER root cause is mapped to a named EBSA best-practice item with a control change raised and reported to the plan committee.

checklist.step: Run the monthly complaint trend and threshold review
actions: Refresh the ERISA complaint dashboard: volume by plan, subtype and provider; complaints per 10,000 participants; SLA attainment; average days to resolution; and open systemic issues past due.
Compare each plan's complaint rate to its own trailing 12-month mean and flag any plan more than two standard deviations above it.
Review every case still open past day 25 by name with the assigned handler and record the reason and the recovery date.
Table the regulator-driven cases separately with their statutory due dates and current status.
Publish the dashboard pack to the Head of Compliance within 5 business days of month end.
checklist.done: the monthly pack is published within 5 business days of month end with outliers flagged and every past-day-25 case explained by name.

checklist.step: Report complaint themes to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee
actions: Prepare the quarterly ERISA complaint paper: volumes and rates by plan, the top three root causes, every systemic issue with owner and due date, regulator referrals received and answered, and cyber incidents affecting participant data.
Set out what the Committee is being asked to decide — provider retention, a plan-document or SPD amendment, a control investment — rather than presenting the pack for noting only.
Load the paper to the board portal at least 5 business days before the meeting so members can read it.
Have the Corporate Secretary minute the Committee's decisions, the dissent if any, and the follow-up owners, because prudence under ERISA §404(a)(1)(B) is proved by the documented process.
Track every Committee action to closure on the ERISA governance action log.
checklist.done: the paper is on the board portal 5 business days ahead, decisions are minuted with owners, and actions are on the governance log.

checklist.step: Retain the complaint file for the ERISA retention period
actions: Export the closed case with its correspondence, chronology, root-cause memo, remediation evidence and any regulator submission into the compliance evidence repository under ERISA / Complaints / <plan number> / <year>.
Apply the 6-year retention label measured from resolution date per ERISA §107, and the indefinite benefit-entitlement label per ERISA §209 where the complaint touched a benefit calculation.
Index the record so it is retrievable by ERISA plan number, participant identifier, subtype and regulator case number.
Confirm the record is under legal hold where litigation or a DOL investigation involving the plan is open, and suppress the retention clock while the hold stands.
Reconcile the monthly count of closed cases to records ingested and chase any difference with the Complaints Specialist within 5 business days.
checklist.done: closed cases are in the repository with the correct ERISA retention label, indexed by plan number, and the monthly closed-to-ingested counts reconcile.

testing.step: Build the population of ERISA complaints closed in the quarter
actions: Extract every case closed in the quarter with a populated ERISA plan number, with columns for receipt date, acknowledgement date, response date, subtype, plan, provider and root cause.

Extract separately every case received in the quarter through the compliance mailbox from EBSA or a state DOI, regardless of subtype coding, so a mis-coded regulator referral cannot fall out of scope.
Add all participant-data incident tickets from SIEM/SOAR that generated participant contact in the quarter and match them to complaint cases.
Reconcile the extract to the contact-centre disposition counts in Genesys Cloud and to the regulator log, and resolve every difference before drawing a sample.
Have the extractor sign the population as complete with the query, the run date and the row count recorded.
testing.done: the population reconciles to contact-centre dispositions, the regulator log and the incident tickets, and is signed as complete.

testing.step: Reconcile the register to the source of record for coding integrity
actions: Match each case's ERISA plan number and sponsor EIN to the recordkeeping system's plan master and flag any that do not exist.
Read the verbatim allegation on 100% of cases coded to a non-ERISA subtype but carrying an ERISA plan number, and flag any that should have been ERISA-coded.
Confirm every case whose allegation words include unauthorised access, phishing, account takeover, wrong statement recipient or lost data carries the ERISA-CYBER subtype and a SIEM/SOAR incident id.
List coding mismatches as automatic exceptions — subtype coding drives the escalation triggers, so a mis-code is a control failure, not a data-quality note.
testing.done: every case's plan identifiers tie to the plan master and every cyber-worded allegation carries the ERISA-CYBER subtype and an incident id, or is listed as an exception.

testing.step: Draw and document a reproducible sample
actions: Take 100% of regulator-driven cases (EBSA and state DOI) and 100% of ERISA-CYBER cases.
Take 25 further cases by seeded random selection stratified across ERISA-CLAIMS, ERISA-FEE and ERISA-SERVICE, for a minimum of 40 rows overall.
Record the random seed, population size, stratum counts and selection date in the workpaper so the same sample can be re-drawn on request.
Confirm no sampled case was handled, reviewed or responded to by the auditor performing the test.
testing.done: the sample is drawn, reproducible from the recorded seed, and covers every regulator-driven and cyber case.

testing.step: Re-perform the escalation-trigger screen without reading the handler's conclusion
actions: Read the verbatim allegation for each sampled case with the handler's trigger screen hidden and reach your own trigger conclusion against ERISA §404(a)(1)(B), §404(e) and the EBSA best-practice list.
Compare your conclusion to the recorded screen; a missed High-severity trigger is an exception even where the outcome for the participant was correct.

Where a trigger fired, verify the timestamped notification actually reached the ERISA Plan Administration Committee secretary, General Counsel or the Chief Info Security Officer within the required window (same business day, or 4 hours for cyber).
Attach your independent screen note and the notification evidence to the workpaper.
testing.done: each sampled case has an independent trigger conclusion and, where triggered, verified notification evidence inside the required window.

testing.step: Recompute the response day counts against the correct clock
actions: Recompute acknowledgement days = acknowledgement send date − receipt date in business days, and response days = substantive response send date − receipt date in calendar days.

For regulator-driven cases, recompute against the date printed on the EBSA or DOI transmittal rather than the internal 30-day default, and read the transmittal itself rather than the case header field.
For cases cross-linked to a claim appeal, confirm the 29 CFR 2560.503-1 appeal decision was issued inside 60 days and that the complaint response did not displace or delay it.
Test the send date against the delivery proof, not the case status change, since a case can be marked responded before the letter goes out.
testing.done: day counts are recomputed from source dates and delivery proof, and every miss against the 2-day, 30-day or regulator date is listed.

testing.step: Trace sampled responses to plan documents and required rights language
actions: Open each sampled response and confirm every distinct allegation in the verbatim text is answered in its own numbered paragraph.
Trace each plan provision quoted to the operative plan document and SPD edition in force on the complaint date and confirm the section number and wording match.

For claim-linked responses, confirm the 29 CFR 2560.503-1(g) content is present — specific reason, plan provision relied on, any internal rule or clinical criterion, and the ERISA §502(a) civil action right.
Treat a response that quotes a superseded SPD edition as a fail, not a formatting point.
testing.done: every sampled response answers each allegation separately, cites the in-force plan document edition and carries the §502(a) rights language where required.

testing.step: Verify the service-provider monitoring evidence behind vendor-named cases
actions: For each sampled case naming a recordkeeper, TPA or custodian, pull the vendor file and confirm it holds the current §408(b)(2) fee disclosure and an in-date SOC 2 Type II report with a bridge letter covering the complaint date.
Confirm a dated written account of the failure was obtained from the provider inside 10 business days and that it names a root cause and a corrective action.
Confirm the complaint is reflected in the vendor scorecard and that providers with two or more substantiated complaints in 12 months were tabled to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee.
Treat a missing provider account or an expired SOC 2 as a prudent-monitoring failure under ERISA §404(a)(1)(B), reportable to the Committee.
testing.done: every vendor-named sampled case shows an in-date SOC 2, a dated provider account and a scorecard entry, or a reported monitoring failure.

testing.step: Re-perform the cyber access determination on ERISA-CYBER cases
actions: Open the linked SIEM/SOAR incident for each ERISA-CYBER case and pull the raw authentication and session logs for the participant account rather than the analyst's summary.
Independently classify the access — participant, authorised delegate, internal user or unknown actor — and compare to the recorded determination.
Confirm containment actions actually applied: distribution and address-change freeze set in the recordkeeping system, credentials reset, and the plan sponsor notified as a fiduciary matter.
Confirm the Privacy Officer assessed state breach-notification obligations and that the assessment date pre-dates any applicable notification deadline.
Capture the log evidence you relied on into the workpaper.
testing.done: each ERISA-CYBER case has an independent access classification with raw log evidence and verified containment and notification actions.

testing.step: Log every exception with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise a GRC issue per exception carrying the case id, plan number, what was missed and the participant or fiduciary impact.

Assign a root cause from the taxonomy — intake miscoded, trigger screen skipped, clock set from the wrong date, superseded SPD used, provider evidence not obtained, containment not applied — and a named process owner.
Set a remediation date of 30 days for regulator-deadline and access-control exceptions and 90 days for process or system changes.
Where a regulator deadline was missed, open a self-report assessment with General Counsel before the next EBSA or DOI contact.
Carry every open issue into the next quarter's test as a mandatory retest row.
testing.done: every exception has a GRC issue, a taxonomy root cause, a named owner, a dated remediation and a retest commitment.

testing.step: Conclude, sign and report the quarterly test
actions: Compute acknowledgement and response attainment against the 98% threshold and count the zero-tolerance failures (regulator deadline missed, cyber case without an incident id, overdue root cause).
State the conclusion — effective, effective with exceptions, or ineffective — with the workpaper reference behind each supporting figure.
Have the independent reviewer, who handled none of the sampled cases and reports outside Market Conduct, sign the workpaper.
Report the conclusion, the exception schedule and any fiduciary-breach or participant-data breaches to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee at its next sitting.
File the signed workpaper in the compliance evidence repository under ERISA / Market Conduct / <quarter> with the 6-year retention label.
testing.done: a signed workpaper with attainment rates, zero-tolerance failures, a stated conclusion and a Committee reporting date is filed in the repository.

Accountable obligation owner.value: Owns the annual ERISA participant-notice audit covering SPD, SMM, SAR, 404(a)(5) fee disclosure, blackout, QDIA and 2560.503-1 claim determination notices; reports the opinion to the Audit Committee and the ERISA Plan Administration Committee.

Citation verified against current regula.value: Yes — 29 CFR 2560.503-1(f)–(l) claim notification timing and content, 29 CFR 2520.104b-2 (SPD within 90 days of coverage), 2520.104b-3 (SMM within 210 days after the plan year of the change), 2520.104b-10 (SAR within 9 months of plan year end, or 2 months after a Form 5500 filed on the 2½-month extension), 2520.101-3 (blackout notice 30–60 days in advance) and 2550.404a-5, each re-read on eCFR at audit planning.

In-scope processes.value: Notice generation, content assembly, print/electronic delivery and proof-of-delivery capture for every ERISA plan administered — retirement, group health, life, disability and long-term care — plus the claim determination and appeal letter production run by Benefits Administration and the claims platform.

In-scope systems.value: Notice masters, edition history and delivery proofs held in the document management repository; generation and address-of-record data from the HRIS and recordkeeping system; claim determination letters from the claims platform; audit workpapers in AuditBoard.

Compliance procedure documented.value: ERISA Notice Audit Programme — scope by notice type and plan, population build from the notice-generation log, sample sizing, the content attribute grid per notice type keyed to its regulation, the day-count recomputation rules, and the exception and reporting protocol.

Compliance procedure approved.value: Audit programme approved by the Chief Audit Executive and accepted by the Audit Committee in the annual plan; the underlying notice content standards are approved by Regulatory Counsel and refreshed on any EBSA regulatory amendment.

Filing/reporting deadlines tracked.value: Audit runs on the plan-year cycle: fieldwork opens after the Form 5500 due date of the last day of the 7th month after plan year end (31 July for calendar plans, 15 October on a Form 5558 extension), tests SAR delivery against the 9-month rule, SMM against 210 days after the plan year of change, and claim notices against the 30/45/90-day determination and 60-day appeal clocks; the audit report is issued within 120 days of fieldwork start.

Deadline reminders configured.value: AuditBoard milestone reminders at planning, fieldwork start, 30-day and 90-day fieldwork checkpoints and report issue; separate calendar alerts on the plan's own notice due dates so the audit tests against live obligations rather than a static list.

Evidence retained per the retention requ.value: Audit workpapers, notice specimens, delivery proofs and day-count recomputations retained 6 years from report issue per ERISA §107, with benefit-determination notices retained as long as relevant to the participant's claim per ERISA §209.

Violations/exceptions logged with dispos.value: Every late or content-defective notice is raised as an AuditBoard finding with rated severity, the population re-issue requirement, a named owner and an agreed date; systemic content defects trigger a full-population re-issue rather than a sample fix.

Remediation sign-off captured.value: Signs the audit opinion and validates closure of every finding by re-testing the corrected notice population before the finding is closed.

Test population (in-scope transactions,.value: All ERISA participant notices generated in the plan year across administered plans — SPD and SMM issues, SARs, annual 404(a)(5) fee disclosures, blackout notices, QDIA and safe-harbor notices, plus all initial claim determination and appeal decision letters produced by the claims platform in the plan year.

Pass/fail thresholds.value: Zero tolerance on timing — any notice delivered after its regulatory deadline is a fail; content attribute accuracy must be 100% on the required elements of 29 CFR 2560.503-1(g) and (j); any notice type with 2 or more content defects in the sample triggers a full-population review; any deemed-exhaustion exposure under 2560.503-1(l) is reported to the Audit Committee immediately.

Compliance test frequency matched to the.value: Obligation is annual for the audit itself and per-event for the underlying notices; the audit is performed once per plan year over the full plan-year population, with a targeted interim re-test of any notice type that failed the prior year.

Independent reviewer (segregated from th.value: A second Internal Auditor with no involvement in the fieldwork reviews the workpapers; no member of Benefits Administration, Retirement Operations or Communications may review or edit the findings.

Evidence location for test results.value: Annual ERISA Notice Audit workpaper set in AuditBoard — population extracts, sample lists with seeds, notice specimens, content attribute grids, day-count recomputations and the finding schedule — with the signed report copied to the compliance evidence repository.

Regulator-ready documentation.value: Signed audit report with the notice inventory, per-notice-type timing results, content attribute grids and the finding register, producible to an EBSA investigator or a plan sponsor's counsel within 10 business days of request.

Regulator response path.value: Chief Audit Executive releases audit findings to a regulator only through General Counsel; Regulatory Counsel decides whether a systemic late-notice finding requires correction under the EBSA Voluntary Fiduciary Correction Program or the Delinquent Filer Voluntary Compliance Program.

checklist.step: Build the notice inventory for every administered ERISA plan
actions: Ask the Benefits Administrator and the Retirement Operations Administrator for the plan list with, for each plan, the three-digit plan number, sponsor EIN, plan year end, participant count at the start of the plan year and large/small plan status.

For each plan, list every ERISA notice it owes: SPD, SMM, SAR, annual 404(a)(5) participant fee disclosure, quarterly benefit statement, blackout notice, QDIA notice, safe-harbor notice, automatic-enrolment notice and 2560.503-1 claim determination and appeal letters.

Against each notice write its regulatory deadline rule and citation — SPD 90 days from becoming covered (29 CFR 2520.104b-2), SMM 210 days after the plan year of the change (2520.104b-3), SAR 9 months after plan year end (2520.104b-10), blackout 30–60 days in advance (2520.101-3).
Mark which notices were actually triggered in the plan year, since a blackout or SMM only exists if an event occurred; obtain the plan amendment log to prove which SMMs were owed.
Load the inventory into AuditBoard as the audit scope and have the Chief Audit Executive approve it before fieldwork.
checklist.done: an approved inventory exists showing, per plan, every notice owed in the plan year with its deadline rule and citation.

checklist.step: Extract the notice-generation population from the source systems
actions: Pull from the HRIS every enrolment event in the plan year — new hires, rehires, coverage elections, terminations, qualifying life events — with the event date that starts each notice clock.

Pull from the recordkeeping and print-vendor logs every notice generated in the plan year with notice type, plan, participant id, generation date, delivery method (mail, electronic under 29 CFR 2520.104b-31, in-hand) and delivery-proof reference.
Pull from the claims platform every initial determination and appeal decision letter issued in the plan year with the claim receipt date, the determination date and any extension notice date.
Reconcile the enrolment-event count to the notices generated: a covered event with no notice row is an immediate exception, not a data gap.
Sign the population extract with the query text, run date and row count and file it in the AuditBoard workpaper.
checklist.done: the notice population reconciles to enrolment events, recordkeeper logs and claims-platform letters, and is signed as complete.

checklist.step: Confirm the notice master editions in force during the plan year
actions: Retrieve from the document management repository every notice master and template edition with its effective-from and effective-to dates for the plan year.
Check each edition against the plan document and any amendment adopted in the year — an amendment with no matching SMM and no SPD or template update is a finding.
Confirm the SPD edition is within the restatement cycle: every 5 years where the plan was amended, every 10 years otherwise, per 29 CFR 2520.104b-2(b).
Record the edition in force on each date so a sampled notice can be tested against the right master, not the current one.
Ask Regulatory Counsel to confirm in writing which editions were counsel-approved and when.
checklist.done: an edition-in-force calendar exists for every notice type with counsel-approval dates and SPD restatement-cycle status recorded.

checklist.step: Build the content attribute grid for each notice type
actions: For claim determination notices, list the 29 CFR 2560.503-1(g) attributes as separate testable lines: specific reason for the denial, reference to the plan provision relied on, description of additional material needed and why, description of the review procedures and time limits, and the statement of the right to bring a civil action under ERISA §502(a).

For appeal decision notices add the 2560.503-1(j) attributes: reference to the internal rule, guideline or protocol relied on or a statement it is available free on request, and for disability claims the additional 2560.503-1(j)(6) content including any disagreement with a treating physician or SSA determination.

For SPDs list the 29 CFR 2520.102-3 required contents and the 2520.102-2 style and comprehension requirements, including the non-English language assistance notice where the participant thresholds are met.
For 404(a)(5) fee disclosures list the plan-level administrative, individual-expense and investment-level fee and performance tables required by 29 CFR 2550.404a-5(c) and (d).
Have Regulatory Counsel review and sign the grids before testing so a content fail cannot later be argued as auditor preference.
checklist.done: each notice type has a counsel-signed attribute grid with one testable line per regulatory element.

checklist.step: Draw the sample and record the selection method
actions: Take 100% of blackout notices, SMMs and SARs issued in the plan year — these are low-volume and each miss is plan-wide.
Take 25 SPDs across plans, weighted to plans with the most new entrants in the year, and 25 annual 404(a)(5) fee disclosures.
Take 40 claim determination letters stratified by plan type — group health, disability and pension have different clocks — plus 100% of appeal decisions that upheld the denial.
Record the random seed, population size per stratum, selection date and the tool used so the sample can be re-drawn identically.
Confirm no sampled notice was drafted, approved or dispatched by anyone on the audit team.
checklist.done: the sample is drawn and reproducible, with full coverage of blackout, SMM, SAR and upheld-appeal populations.

checklist.step: Test the timing of each sampled notice against its own clock
actions: For each sampled SPD, recompute delivery date − date the participant became covered and test against the 90-day rule; for a new plan test against 120 days after the plan became subject to ERISA.
For each SMM, recompute delivery date − the last day of the plan year in which the modification was adopted and test against 210 days.
For each SAR, recompute delivery date − plan year end and test against 9 months, extending to 2 months after the actual Form 5500 filing only where a valid Form 5558 extension is on file.

For each blackout notice, recompute the days between delivery and the blackout start and test it falls inside the 30-to-60-day window, and where fewer than 30 days confirm the plan fiduciary's written 2520.101-3(b)(2) determination exists.
Take the delivery date from the print vendor's mail-date file or the electronic delivery receipt, never from the document's own header date.
checklist.done: every sampled notice has a recomputed day count taken from delivery proof and a pass/fail against its cited rule.

checklist.step: Test claim determination timing against the 2560.503-1 clocks
actions: Take the claim receipt date from the claims platform intake timestamp, not the adjudicator's assignment date.
Recompute the determination interval against the applicable rule: 15 days for pre-service group health, 30 days post-service, 45 days for disability, 90 days for pension claims.

Where an extension was used, confirm the extension notice was issued before the original period expired, states the standards on which entitlement is based, the unresolved issues and the additional information needed, and that only the permitted number of extensions was taken (one 15-day for group health, two 30-day for disability).

Where the participant was asked for information, confirm the tolling period was applied only for the days the claim was actually pending the participant's response and that the participant was given at least 45 days to respond.
Recompute appeal decision intervals against the 60-day pension and disability rules and the group health 15/30-day rules.
checklist.done: every sampled determination and appeal has a recomputed interval from platform timestamps, with extension and tolling validity separately proved.

checklist.step: Test notice content line by line against the attribute grid
actions: Open each sampled notice specimen as it was sent — the merged, participant-specific output, not the template.
Mark each attribute grid line present or absent, and quote the sentence in the notice that satisfies it; an attribute with no quotable sentence is absent.
For denial letters, confirm the reason is specific to this claim rather than a generic 'not medically necessary' or 'not covered under the plan' without the provision cited.
Confirm the ERISA §502(a) civil action statement is present and unqualified, and that the review procedures paragraph states the actual time limits.
Flag readability failures under 29 CFR 2520.102-2 — undefined technical terms, absent non-English assistance notice where the participant counts require it — as content defects.
checklist.done: each sampled notice has a completed attribute grid with a quoted sentence behind every attribute marked present.

checklist.step: Prove delivery actually reached the participant of record
actions: Match the address or email used on each sampled notice to the address of record in the HRIS and recordkeeping system on the send date.

For electronic delivery, confirm the 29 CFR 2520.104b-31 notice-and-access conditions were met: an initial paper notification of default electronic delivery, a working right to opt out on paper, and a system that alerts on invalid or inoperable addresses.
Pull the bounce, undeliverable and returned-mail report for the sampled notices and confirm each return was worked to a re-issue with a documented address search.
Confirm the delivery proof reference on the notice row resolves to an actual vendor record, not a null or placeholder.
Treat a notice delivered to a stale address that later bounced with no re-issue as a non-delivery, not a delivery.
checklist.done: every sampled notice ties to an address of record, a valid electronic-delivery basis where used, and a worked return where it bounced.

checklist.step: Test the 404(a)(5) and 408(b)(2) disclosure cycle
actions: Confirm each participant received an annual 404(a)(5) disclosure at least once in any 14-month period and quarterly statements of fees actually charged to the account.
Trace the plan-level and investment-level fee figures in the disclosure back to the recordkeeper billing file and the fund fact sheets for the period.

Confirm the covered service provider disclosures under 29 CFR 2550.408b-2(c) are on file for every provider reasonably in advance of the contract, with changes disclosed within 60 days of the date the provider is informed of them.
Where a provider disclosure is missing, confirm the plan fiduciary made the written request required by 2550.408b-2(c)(1)(ix) and, if unanswered within 90 days, reported the provider to EBSA.
Report any gap as a prohibited-transaction exposure to General Counsel, not as a documentation observation.
checklist.done: the 14-month participant cycle and every covered provider disclosure are evidenced, with any gap escalated to counsel as a prohibited-transaction exposure.

checklist.step: Assess the deemed-exhaustion exposure from any procedural failure
actions: Review every timing or content failure the audit found against 29 CFR 2560.503-1(l): a failure to establish or follow procedures in accordance with the section lets the claimant treat the internal remedies as exhausted and sue under §502(a).

Judge whether the failure is de minimis under 2560.503-1(l)(2)(ii) — non-prejudicial, attributable to good cause or matters beyond the plan's control, in the context of an ongoing good-faith exchange — and record the reasoning, not just the conclusion.
Quantify the exposed population: how many participants received the defective notice and how many are still inside the limitation period.
Advise whether the affected participants must be re-notified with a fresh appeal right, and set the date by which the re-issue must go out.
Brief the ERISA Plan Administration Committee and the Audit Committee in writing on any exposure judged more than de minimis.
checklist.done: each procedural failure has a written de minimis analysis, a quantified exposed population and a decision on re-notification.

checklist.step: Raise findings with severity, population impact and owners
actions: Raise one AuditBoard finding per control failure — not per sampled notice — with the sample failure rate and the projected population impact stated.

Rate severity: Critical for any deemed-exhaustion exposure or plan-wide missing SAR, blackout or SMM; High for content attributes absent from 2560.503-1 letters; Medium for delivery-proof and address-hygiene failures.
Name the accountable owner from Benefits Administration, Retirement Operations, Communications or the recordkeeper relationship, and agree the remediation date in writing with them.
Require full-population re-issue where a template defect is the cause, since every notice off that template carries the same defect.
Confirm the owner's response states the closure evidence — a re-issue file with delivery proofs, a counsel-approved template edition, or a re-run control test.
checklist.done: every control failure has a rated finding with projected population impact, a named owner, an agreed date and pre-stated closure evidence.

checklist.step: Issue the audit report and take it to both committees
actions: Issue the report within 120 days of fieldwork start with a stated opinion per notice type, the timing attainment rates and the content attribute results.
Set out the deemed-exhaustion exposure and counsel's position on it in its own section — this is the fiduciary risk, not a technical annexe.
Load the report to the board portal for the ERISA Plan Administration Committee and the Audit Committee at least 5 business days before their meetings.
Ask the Corporate Secretary to minute the committees' acceptance, the remediation dates agreed and any decision to re-notify participants.
Publish the finding register to the owners with the agreed dates the day the report issues.
checklist.done: the report is issued within 120 days, tabled at both committees with 5 business days' notice, and the decisions are minuted.

checklist.step: Validate remediation before closing any finding
actions: Re-test each remediated notice type on a fresh sample drawn after the fix date, using the same attribute grid.
For template fixes, confirm the new edition is in the document management repository with a counsel approval date and that the old edition is retired so it cannot be merged again.
For re-issue commitments, reconcile the re-issued population count to the exposed population count identified in the finding and confirm delivery proofs exist for each.
Close the finding only on evidence; an owner's assertion that the fix is in production is not closure evidence.
Report any finding past its agreed date to the Audit Committee with the number of days overdue.
checklist.done: each finding is closed only after a post-fix re-test, a retired old edition and a re-issue count reconciled to the exposed population.

checklist.step: Retain the audit file for the ERISA retention period
actions: Export the complete workpaper set — inventory, population extracts, sample seeds, notice specimens, attribute grids, day-count recomputations, counsel analyses and the signed report — from AuditBoard to the compliance evidence repository under ERISA / Notice Audit / <plan year>.
Apply the 6-year retention label from report issue per ERISA §107 and the indefinite label per ERISA §209 on any workpaper holding a benefit determination notice.
Index the file so it is retrievable by plan number, notice type and plan year for an EBSA investigator or a plan sponsor's counsel.
Apply a legal hold and suspend the retention clock where a §502(a) claim or a DOL investigation touching the plan is open.
Confirm the repository index resolves and record the ingestion date on the audit closure memo.
checklist.done: the full workpaper set is in the repository with ERISA retention labels, indexed by plan number, notice type and plan year.

testing.step: Rebuild the notice population independently of the audit team
actions: Re-run the enrolment-event extract from the HRIS for the plan year using your own query and compare the row count to the audit's population.
Re-pull the notice-generation log from the recordkeeper and print vendor and compare notice counts by type and plan.
Re-pull the plan amendment log and confirm every amendment adopted in the year appears in the audit's SMM population.
Investigate and document any difference above zero before relying on the audit's coverage — an under-built population makes every downstream conclusion untestable.
testing.done: the independently rebuilt population agrees to the audit population by type and plan, with every difference explained in writing.

testing.step: Reconcile the notice inventory to the plan documents that create the obligations
actions: Read each administered plan's document and adoption agreement and list the notices that plan design actually triggers — automatic enrolment, QDIA, safe harbor, participant-directed investment.
Compare to the audit's inventory and flag any owed notice the audit never scoped.
Confirm each inventory line carries the correct citation and that the deadline rule quoted matches the current eCFR text rather than a legacy internal standard.
Treat a notice type absent from scope as a scope failure reportable to the Audit Committee, ranking above any individual sample exception.
testing.done: every notice the plan documents trigger appears in the audit inventory with a citation matching current eCFR text, or a scope failure is reported.

testing.step: Re-draw the sample from the recorded seed and confirm coverage
actions: Re-run the selection using the seed, population size and stratum counts recorded in the workpaper and compare the resulting item list to the audit's sample.
Confirm 100% coverage was actually achieved on blackout notices, SMMs, SARs and upheld appeal decisions rather than sampled.
Confirm the claim-determination stratification covers group health, disability and pension, since each has a different clock and a single-stratum sample proves nothing about the others.
List any sampled item that cannot be re-derived from the seed as a sampling-integrity exception.
testing.done: the sample re-draws identically from the recorded seed and full-population coverage is confirmed on the low-volume notice types.

testing.step: Re-perform the day-count maths on a sub-sample from source dates
actions: Take 15 sampled notices across SPD, SMM, SAR and blackout and recompute each day count from the underlying event date and the vendor mail-date file without looking at the audit's figure.

Confirm the correct rule was applied to each: 90 days from coverage for SPD, 210 days from the plan year of adoption for SMM, 9 months from plan year end for SAR, and the 30-to-60-day window for blackout.
Where a SAR relied on the extended deadline, open the Form 5558 and confirm it was filed by the original Form 5500 due date and that the 2-month extension runs from the actual filing date.
Any difference between your count and the audit's is an exception, including a right answer reached from the wrong start date.
testing.done: each re-performed day count agrees with the audit's or is listed as an exception with both computations shown.

testing.step: Re-perform the content attribute test on denial and appeal letters
actions: Take 10 sampled claim determination letters and 10 upheld appeal decisions and mark the 2560.503-1(g) and (j) attributes yourself with the audit's grid hidden.
Require a quotable sentence for each attribute marked present and record it; an attribute the auditor passed on inference is an exception.

For disability appeals, confirm the 2560.503-1(j)(6) elements are present, including any explanation of disagreement with a treating physician's view or a Social Security Administration disability determination in the file.
Compare your grid to the audit's and treat every difference as an exception in the audit's content testing, separate from the underlying notice defect.
testing.done: an independent attribute grid exists for 20 letters with quoted sentences, and every difference from the audit's grid is listed.

testing.step: Trace delivery proof to the vendor record and the address of record
actions: Open the delivery-proof reference on 20 sampled notices in the document management repository and confirm it resolves to an actual print-vendor mail-date record or electronic delivery receipt.
Compare the address or email used to the address of record held on the send date and confirm they match.
For electronic delivery, confirm the participant's initial paper notification, opt-out right and the invalid-address alerting required by 29 CFR 2520.104b-31 are all evidenced.
Pull the returned-mail report and confirm each sampled return was re-issued after an address search, and treat any un-worked return as a non-delivery exception.
testing.done: every traced notice resolves to a real vendor delivery record at the address of record, with the electronic-delivery conditions evidenced where used.

testing.step: Test the fee-disclosure cycle independently of the audit
actions: Select 15 participants and compute the interval between their last two 404(a)(5) annual disclosures, testing against the 14-month maximum.
Trace the plan-level administrative expense figure on one disclosure to the recordkeeper's billing invoices for the period and confirm the total agrees.
Trace two investment-level expense ratios to the fund prospectus or fact sheet in force for the period.
Confirm quarterly statements show the dollar amounts of fees actually deducted from the account and reconcile to the account transaction history.
List any interval over 14 months or unreconciled figure as an exception and route it to General Counsel for prohibited-transaction assessment.
testing.done: every tested participant's disclosure interval is inside 14 months and disclosed fees reconcile to billing and fund source data, or are listed as exceptions.

testing.step: Verify the deemed-exhaustion analysis and the exposed population count
actions: Read counsel's 2560.503-1(l) analysis for each procedural failure and confirm it addresses whether the failure was non-prejudicial, for good cause or beyond the plan's control, and part of an ongoing good-faith exchange.
Recompute the exposed population by re-querying the notice log for every participant who received the defective template edition, not just those sampled.
Confirm the re-notification decision and its date, and that re-notified participants were given a fresh appeal period.
Treat an analysis that concludes de minimis without addressing prejudice to the claimant as unsupported, and require it to be re-done.
testing.done: each exhaustion analysis addresses every 2560.503-1(l)(2)(ii) element and the exposed population is independently recomputed from the notice log.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise a GRC issue per exception with the notice type, plan number, participants affected and whether the failure is timing, content, delivery or scope.

Assign a root cause — template edition not updated after amendment, clock started from the wrong event date, extension notice issued late, address of record stale, notice type never scoped — and a named owner in the process that failed.
Set 30 days for re-notification and template corrections and 90 days for system or data changes, and record the closure evidence required up front.
Escalate any Critical-rated exhaustion exposure to the Audit Committee within 5 business days rather than waiting for the report cycle.
Carry every open issue into the next plan year's audit scope as a mandatory retest line.
testing.done: every exception carries a GRC issue with root cause, named owner, dated remediation and a retest line in next year's scope.

testing.step: Conclude, obtain independent sign-off and report
actions: Compute per-notice-type timing attainment and content attribute accuracy and compare them to the zero-tolerance timing and 100% content thresholds.
State the conclusion — effective, effective with exceptions, or ineffective — separately for each notice type, with the workpaper reference behind every figure.
Have a second Internal Auditor with no fieldwork involvement review the workpapers and sign, and confirm no Benefits Administration or Retirement Operations reviewer touched the findings.
Report the conclusion, the exception schedule and the exhaustion exposure to the Audit Committee and the ERISA Plan Administration Committee at their next sittings.
File the signed conclusion memo and workpaper set in the compliance evidence repository with the 6-year ERISA §107 retention label.
testing.done: a signed conclusion memo stating a per-notice-type opinion, attainment rates and committee reporting dates is filed in the repository.

Accountable obligation owner.value: Owns the ERISA fiduciary governance structure — the named fiduciary designations under ERISA §402(a), the Plan Administration and Investment Committee charters, the delegation resolutions under §405(c), the appeals fiduciary appointment under 29 CFR 2560.503-1(b), and the §412 fidelity bond schedule.

Citation verified against current regula.value: Yes — ERISA §402(a) and §402(b)(2) plan-document and fiduciary-allocation requirements, §405(c) delegation, 29 CFR 2560.503-1(b) written claims procedures described in the SPD, ERISA §412 with 29 CFR 2580 bonding rules, and ERISA §209 (29 U.S.C. §1059) records of service, compensation and benefits, each re-read on eCFR at every charter review.

In-scope processes.value: Fiduciary appointment and removal, committee charter drafting and review, meeting calendaring and quorum, agenda and paper distribution, minute-taking and approval, delegation and sub-delegation records, fidelity bond placement and renewal, and the ERISA §209 participant record retention that the committee is accountable for.

In-scope systems.value: Charters, agendas, papers, resolutions and approved minutes held in the board portal with per-committee access and an unalterable version history; executed delegation deeds and the fidelity bond in iManage (Legal Docs); the governance action log in the GRC platform.

Compliance procedure documented.value: ERISA Plan Governance Procedure — how a named fiduciary is appointed and accepts in writing, what each committee must decide versus note, quorum and conflict-recusal rules, the standing agenda that guarantees the annual cycle, minute content standards evidencing a prudent process, and the delegation and bonding registers.

Compliance procedure approved.value: Charters and the governance procedure approved by the Board of Directors as plan sponsor and re-approved annually; General Counsel confirms each charter against the operative plan document and any amendment before re-approval.

Filing/reporting deadlines tracked.value: Continuous with fixed anchors: Plan Administration Committee meets quarterly and the Investment Committee quarterly; charters reviewed annually; minutes drafted within 10 business days of the meeting and approved at the next meeting; fidelity bond renewed before expiry and re-sized within 30 days of any increase in funds handled; Schedule H/I bonding answers confirmed before the Form 5500 due date of the last day of the 7th month after plan year end.

Deadline reminders configured.value: Board portal calendar invitations issued 12 months ahead for every committee sitting with paper cut-off at meeting minus 5 business days; GRC platform reminders at 90, 60 and 30 days before fidelity bond expiry and 30 days before each annual charter review.

Evidence retained per the retention requ.value: Charters, appointment and acceptance letters, delegation deeds, agendas, papers, approved minutes and bond documents retained 6 years per ERISA §107 and permanently where they evidence a benefit-affecting decision, per the ERISA §209 duty to keep records sufficient to determine benefits due.

Violations/exceptions logged with dispos.value: Inquorate meetings, unapproved or late minutes, lapsed appointments, undocumented sub-delegations and an under-sized or lapsed fidelity bond are raised as governance issues with owner, due date and closure evidence.

Remediation sign-off captured.value: Signs off remediation of every governance defect and confirms in writing that any retrospective ratification of an act taken without authority is legally effective under the plan document.

Test population (in-scope transactions,.value: All ERISA plan committee and board meetings held in the year, all fiduciary appointments, resignations and removals, all delegation and sub-delegation instruments in force, every charter edition, and the fidelity bond schedule for every plan required to be bonded.

Pass/fail thresholds.value: Zero tolerance — any plan with no named fiduciary in the plan document, any decision taken without quorum, any fiduciary acting with no written acceptance, or any plan whose bond is below the ERISA §412 minimum of 10% of funds handled is a fail; minutes must be approved within one meeting cycle with at least 95% attainment.

Compliance test frequency matched to the.value: Obligation is continuous; a governance attribute test runs semi-annually over the meetings and appointments in the period, with an annual full review of charters, delegations and the bond schedule timed before the Form 5500 Schedule H/I bonding answer is signed.

Independent reviewer (segregated from th.value: Reviewer must not sit in the Corporate Secretariat and must not have drafted, minuted or attended as secretary any meeting in the sample.

Evidence location for test results.value: Semi-annual ERISA governance test workpaper — meeting register, quorum recomputation, minute-content grid, appointment and delegation trace, bond adequacy calculation and exception schedule — filed in the compliance evidence repository under ERISA / Governance / <period>.

Regulator-ready documentation.value: Fiduciary governance pack — plan document fiduciary provisions, current charters, appointment and acceptance letters, delegation deeds, two years of approved minutes and the fidelity bond — producible to an EBSA investigator or a plan auditor within 10 business days.

Regulator response path.value: Corporate Secretary assembles the pack; General Counsel is the single channel to EBSA and decides whether a governance defect that caused a fiduciary act requires correction through the EBSA Voluntary Fiduciary Correction Program.

checklist.step: Read the plan document and list who it names as fiduciary
actions: Open the operative plan document and adoption agreement for each ERISA plan in iManage and read the fiduciary article.

Record, per plan, the named fiduciary under ERISA §402(a)(1), the plan administrator, the trustee, the investment fiduciary and the person or committee designated to decide claims and appeals under 29 CFR 2560.503-1(b).
Confirm the document contains the §402(b)(2) procedure allowing named fiduciaries to allocate responsibilities and to designate others to carry them out — without it, any delegation is void.
Flag any plan whose document names an individual by job title that no longer exists, or a committee that has never been constituted.
Give the Corporate Secretary a written schedule of named fiduciaries per plan with the document section behind each.
checklist.done: a per-plan schedule of named fiduciaries exists, each tied to a plan-document section, with defunct designations flagged.

checklist.step: Constitute or refresh each committee charter
actions: Draft or refresh the Plan Administration Committee and Investment Committee charters stating purpose, the plans in scope, membership by role, quorum, meeting frequency, decision rights reserved to the committee, matters escalated to the Board and reporting lines.

Write the ERISA duties into the charter explicitly: prudence under §404(a)(1)(B), exclusive benefit under §404(a)(1)(A), plan-document compliance under §404(a)(1)(D) and prudent selection and monitoring of service providers under §404(e).

Set the standing annual agenda inside the charter — investment review, service provider and fee review, cybersecurity report, complaint and claims-appeals report, Form 5500 and audit review, charter and bond review — so the cycle cannot silently lapse.
Circulate the draft to General Counsel and the Head of Compliance for comment with a 10-business-day window and record their sign-off.
Publish the approved charter to the board portal with an edition number and effective date and retire the prior edition.
checklist.done: each committee has a current, board-approved charter on the portal with quorum, decision rights and the standing annual agenda stated.

checklist.step: Appoint fiduciaries by resolution and take written acceptance
actions: Prepare a board or committee resolution naming each appointee, the plan, the fiduciary role and the effective date.
Send each appointee an appointment letter that states the ERISA fiduciary duties they are assuming, the personal liability under ERISA §409 and the §411 disqualification criteria.
Obtain the appointee's signed acceptance through DocuSign before they take any decision, and file the executed acceptance in iManage against the plan.
Update the fiduciary register with appointee, plan, role, effective date, acceptance date and the resolution reference.
Where a fiduciary resigns or leaves the company, pass the removal resolution the same month and record the exact date their authority ended, so no gap or overlap exists.
checklist.done: every acting fiduciary has a resolution, a signed acceptance dated before their first decision, and a register entry with start and end dates.

checklist.step: Document every delegation and sub-delegation in writing
actions: For each function carried out by someone other than the named fiduciary — recordkeeping, claims adjudication, investment management, custody — draft a delegation instrument under the plan's §402(b)(2) procedure.

State in each instrument the scope delegated, the standard of performance, the reporting owed back to the delegating fiduciary and the monitoring the fiduciary will perform, because §405(c)(2) leaves the delegator liable for imprudent selection or monitoring.
Where an investment manager is appointed, confirm the appointee qualifies as an ERISA §3(38) investment manager and has acknowledged fiduciary status in writing.
Record every instrument in the delegation register with parties, scope, effective date, review date and the monitoring report it produces.
Terminate and archive instruments for functions brought back in house rather than leaving them live.
checklist.done: every delegated function has an executed instrument naming scope, monitoring and reporting, and appears on the delegation register.

checklist.step: Set the twelve-month meeting calendar and paper cut-offs
actions: Issue calendar invitations for all four Plan Administration Committee and four Investment Committee sittings twelve months ahead, aligned to the plan year so the Form 5500 and audit items land before their deadlines.
Set a paper cut-off at meeting minus 5 business days in the board portal and configure it to reject late uploads to the meeting pack rather than silently accepting them.
Book the standing attendees named in the charter plus the standing invitees — the plan auditor, the recordkeeper relationship manager and the Chief Info Security Officer for the cyber item.
Publish the annual agenda map showing which standing item lands at which sitting.
Escalate to the Corporate Secretary any sitting that would fall outside the charter's frequency so it is rescheduled, never dropped.
checklist.done: a twelve-month calendar with paper cut-offs and the standing agenda map is published on the board portal for both committees.

checklist.step: Assemble each meeting pack against the standing agenda
actions: Build the agenda from the charter's standing items plus any matter escalated on the governance action log.

Collect the papers from their owners: investment performance and fee review from the Investment Operations Manager, service provider and 408(b)(2) fee report from the Third-Party Risk Manager, cybersecurity report from the Chief Info Security Officer, claims-appeal and complaint report from Market Conduct, and the Form 5500 and plan audit status from the Controller.
Require each paper to state the decision sought, the options considered and the recommendation, since prudence is evidenced by the alternatives weighed not by the outcome.
Upload the pack to the board portal by the cut-off and record any paper that missed it, with the reason, on the meeting file.
Circulate the pack link with a read receipt so member preparation is evidenced.
checklist.done: the pack is on the portal by the cut-off, each paper states the decision sought and the options considered, and read receipts are captured.

checklist.step: Test and record quorum and conflicts at the start of every meeting
actions: Take the attendance register at the start, distinguishing members from attendees and noting the joining and leaving time of anyone partially present.
Compare the member count to the quorum stated in the charter and record whether quorum was met before any decision is taken.
Invite conflict declarations against the agenda items, record each declaration and the recusal decision, and note the recused member leaving and rejoining.
Where quorum fails, restrict the meeting to discussion only and calendar a reconvened sitting or a written resolution to take the decisions.
Never record a decision as taken at an inquorate meeting — the decision is void and any act on it is an unauthorised fiduciary act.
checklist.done: each meeting file shows the attendance register, an explicit quorum determination before decisions, and every declared conflict with its recusal.

checklist.step: Minute the decision process, not just the decision
actions: Draft minutes within 10 business days recording, for each decision: the question, the options presented, the data and advice relied on with the paper reference, the discussion points, any dissent, the resolution passed and the vote.
Name the adviser or provider whose analysis was relied on and attach it, because ERISA §404(a)(1)(B) prudence is judged on the process behind the decision.
Record the action items with owner and due date and push them straight to the governance action log.
Circulate the draft to attendees for factual correction with a 5-business-day window and keep the correction trail.
Table the minutes for approval at the next sitting and mark them Approved with the date, since unapproved minutes are not evidence of a prudent process.
checklist.done: minutes drafted within 10 business days show options, advice relied on, dissent and vote for each decision, and are approved at the next sitting.

checklist.step: Maintain the claims and appeals fiduciary appointment
actions: Confirm the person or committee that decides appeals is the one named in the plan document and the SPD, and that the SPD text describing the claims procedure matches the procedure actually run.
Confirm the appeals decider is not the person who made the initial adverse determination and is not that person's subordinate, as 29 CFR 2560.503-1(h)(3)(ii) requires.
Where a medical judgement is involved, confirm the consulting health care professional engaged for the appeal was not consulted on the initial denial and was not that consultant's subordinate.
Keep the roster of appeal deciders and consulting professionals current, with the effective dates each served, so any decision can be tied to an authorised decider.
Report any appeal decided by an unauthorised person to General Counsel immediately as a 2560.503-1(l) exposure.
checklist.done: the appeals decider matches the plan document and SPD, independence from the initial decider is evidenced, and the decider roster carries effective dates.

checklist.step: Place and size the ERISA §412 fidelity bond
actions: List every person who handles plan funds or other property — committee members, benefit payment approvers, contribution remitters and any service provider not exempt — from the fiduciary and delegation registers.

Compute the required bond per plan as 10% of the funds handled in the preceding plan year, with a $1,000 floor and a $500,000 cap, rising to $1,000,000 where the plan holds employer securities, per ERISA §412 and 29 CFR 2580.
Confirm the bond names the plan as insured, is written by a Treasury-listed surety, has no deductible against the plan, and covers the full plan year with no gap at renewal.
Re-size the bond within 30 days of any material increase in funds handled rather than waiting for renewal.
File the bond and the calculation in iManage and give the Controller the figures for the Form 5500 Schedule H or I bonding questions.
checklist.done: each plan has a Treasury-listed bond at or above 10% of funds handled with no deductible, no gap, and a filed calculation supporting the Form 5500 answer.

checklist.step: Keep the ERISA §209 participant records the committee is accountable for
actions: Confirm with the Retirement Operations Administrator and Payroll Specialist that service, compensation and contribution records exist for every participant for every year of participation, as ERISA §209 requires records sufficient to determine benefits due or that may become due.
Reconcile the recordkeeper's participant service history to payroll source data annually and investigate any participant with missing service years.

Apply an indefinite retention label to service, compensation and beneficiary designation records rather than the general 6-year ERISA §107 label, since benefit entitlement can be tested decades later.
Confirm records survive recordkeeper changes by requiring a full historical data extract at every conversion and validating record counts before the old provider is decommissioned.
Report any gap in participant service history to the Plan Administration Committee as a benefit-determination risk.
checklist.done: participant service and compensation records reconcile to payroll, carry an indefinite retention label, and any gap is reported to the Committee.

checklist.step: Run the annual charter, membership and delegation review
actions: Table each charter for annual review against the current plan document, any amendment adopted in the year, and the actual decisions the committee took.
Review membership against the charter's role-based composition and confirm every seat is filled by a person with a live acceptance letter.
Review every delegation instrument against the monitoring reports it produced — a delegation with no monitoring evidence is an ERISA §405(c)(2) exposure, not a paperwork gap.
Assess committee effectiveness against attendance rates, paper timeliness, decisions deferred and actions overdue, and record the assessment.
Take the reviewed charters to the Board for re-approval and minute the approval.
checklist.done: every charter, seat and delegation is reviewed against actual activity and re-approved by the Board with the approval minuted.

checklist.step: Track governance actions to closure
actions: Load every minuted action item into the GRC governance action log with owner, due date, the minute reference and the closure evidence required.
Chase owners at 14 days and 3 days before due and escalate anything overdue to the committee chair the day it slips.
