actions: List every policy that governs an ERISA fiduciary function: fiduciary governance policy, investment policy statement, service provider selection and monitoring policy, participant claims and appeals procedure, participant fee disclosure policy, cybersecurity program policy, business resiliency policy, record retention and ERISA §209 policy, and the plan expense and settlor-versus-fiduciary expense policy.

Record against each the policy owner, the approval body (Board or ERISA Plan Administration Committee), the current edition number, its effective date, the date of last approval and the next due date twelve months on.
Map each policy to the ERISA provision it implements — §404(a)(1)(B), §404(a)(1)(D), §404(e), 29 CFR 2560.503-1(b), 2550.404a-5, 2550.408b-2(c) — so the inventory shows why the policy exists.
Identify orphan policies with no named owner and unmapped ERISA duties with no policy, and raise both to the Board Governance Lead.
Publish the inventory to the board portal and lock edits to the Governance Analyst and Corporate Secretary.
checklist.done: the inventory lists every ERISA governance policy with owner, approval body, edition, last approval, next due date and the ERISA provision it implements.

checklist.step: Build the annual review calendar across the committee sittings
actions: Assign each policy to one of the four committee sittings so the load is spread and no policy passes 12 months since its last approval.

Sequence dependent policies together — the investment policy statement with the service provider monitoring policy, the claims procedure with the SPD update cycle — so a change in one is reflected in the other in the same cycle.
Back off the milestones from each target sitting: gap assessment at 90 days, redline and legal review at 45 days, committee recommendation at 30 days, papers to the portal at 5 business days.
Issue the calendar to every policy owner with their dates and load the reminders into the board portal.
Reserve capacity at each sitting for an out-of-cycle policy change forced by a regulatory development, so a new EBSA release does not wait for the annual slot.
checklist.done: every policy has a target sitting and back-off milestones on the board portal calendar, with no policy scheduled beyond 12 months from last approval.

checklist.step: Run the gap assessment against current regulatory text
actions: Open the current eCFR text of every regulation the policy implements and the current EBSA guidance page, and record the version date you read.
Compare the policy clause by clause to the regulatory text and list every gap, every superseded reference and every clause that states a standard weaker than the regulation.
Check the DOL EBSA newsroom, Field Assistance Bulletins, Compliance Assistance Releases and Advisory Opinions issued since the last review for anything that changes the expected standard.

Check the policy against the operative plan documents, since ERISA §404(a)(1)(D) requires the plan to be run in accordance with its documents and a policy that contradicts the plan is a breach waiting to happen.
Write the gap assessment memo with a gap list, a materiality rating and a recommended change for each, and file it against the policy on the board portal.
checklist.done: a dated gap assessment memo exists per policy, citing the eCFR and guidance versions read, with a rated gap list and recommended changes.

checklist.step: Test the policy against what actually happens
actions: Walk the policy with the teams that operate it — Benefits Administration, Retirement Operations, the CISO organisation, Third-Party Risk — and record where practice differs from the written policy.
Pull the prior year's exceptions, complaints, audit findings and incidents attributable to the policy area and identify which were caused by the policy rather than by execution.

Decide for each divergence whether practice should change or the policy should — never leave a knowing divergence unresolved, since operating outside an approved policy is itself evidence of an imprudent process.
Where a policy sets a standard the organisation cannot meet, say so in the recommendation paper rather than approving an aspirational policy.
Record the walkthrough participants, dates and findings in the review file.
checklist.done: the review file records a dated walkthrough with operating teams, the divergences found, and a decision to change either the practice or the policy for each.

checklist.step: Draft the redline and route it for functional review
actions: Produce a tracked-change redline of the approved edition rather than a clean rewrite, so the approvers can see exactly what changes.
Attach a change table listing each change, the gap or divergence it answers, and the regulatory citation behind it.

Route to the functional reviewers named in the procedure — the Chief Info Security Officer for the cybersecurity policy, the Chief Investment Officer for the investment policy statement, the Head of Compliance for the claims procedure — with a 10-business-day window.
Record every review comment and its disposition, including comments rejected and why, because the disposition record is part of the prudent-process evidence.
Freeze the draft at 45 days before the sitting and send it to General Counsel for legal review.
checklist.done: a tracked redline with a citation-backed change table exists, functional comments are dispositioned in writing, and the draft is frozen 45 days before the sitting.

checklist.step: Obtain legal review and confirm plan-document alignment
actions: Review the redline against the gap assessment and confirm every material gap is closed or that the residual is explicitly accepted in the recommendation paper.
Confirm the policy does not conflict with the operative plan documents, the SPD or any collective bargaining agreement, and identify any plan amendment or SMM the change will require.
Confirm that any policy describing the claims procedure matches the SPD text word for word in substance, since 29 CFR 2560.503-1(b) requires the SPD to describe the procedures actually used.
Note in writing where a change creates a new obligation with a lead time — a new notice, a new disclosure, a new provider contract term — so implementation is planned, not assumed.
Sign the legal review and file it in iManage against the policy edition.
checklist.done: a signed legal review confirms gap closure, plan-document and SPD alignment, and names any amendment, SMM or lead-time obligation the change creates.

checklist.step: Write the recommendation paper the approvers can actually decide on
actions: State at the top what is being asked for — approve, approve with amendment, or defer — and the date the current edition lapses if no decision is taken.
Summarise the gap assessment findings, the divergences found in operation, the options considered and the recommendation, with the alternatives explicitly set out rather than implied.
Attach the redline, the change table, the gap assessment memo and the legal review as annexes.
State the implementation plan: publication date, communication route, training, system or contract changes, and the owner and date for each.
Submit to the board portal by the 5-business-day cut-off; a paper that misses the cut-off is deferred to the next sitting rather than tabled late.
checklist.done: the paper states the decision sought, the lapse date, the options considered, the recommendation and an owned implementation plan, and is on the portal by the cut-off.

checklist.step: Take the policy to the approval body and minute the decision
actions: Confirm quorum before the policy item is taken and record it, since an approval taken inquorate is void.
Minute the question, the options presented, the discussion, any dissent, the resolution and the vote — an approval minuted as noted rather than resolved is not an approval.
Record the approved edition number, the effective date and any condition or amendment the body directed.
Where the body defers, record the reason, the additional information required and the date the item returns, and confirm the current edition remains in force meanwhile.
Issue the signed resolution to the policy owner within 2 business days of the meeting.
checklist.done: the minute records quorum, options, dissent, the resolution and the vote, and names the approved edition number, effective date and any conditions.

checklist.step: Publish the approved edition and retire the prior one
actions: Publish the approved edition to the policy library within 10 business days of approval, stamped with the edition number, approval date, effective date and approving body.
Move the prior edition to the archive with its effective-to date set, and remove every link that still points at it, since a live link to a superseded policy will be relied on.
Confirm the published file is byte-identical in content to the edition the minute approved, with no post-approval editorial changes.
Notify the operating teams, the recordkeeper and any service provider whose contract references the policy, and give them the effective date.
Update the inventory with the new edition, approval date and the next due date twelve months on.
checklist.done: the approved edition is published within 10 business days, matches the minuted edition exactly, the prior edition is archived with an effective-to date, and the inventory is updated.

checklist.step: Drive acknowledgement and training where the change bites
actions: Identify the target population for each policy from the role map — plan committee members, benefits and retirement operations staff, claims appeal deciders, trust payment authorisers.
Assign the acknowledgement task in the learning management system with a 30-day due date and a link to the published edition.
Where the change alters how work is done, build a short module covering the change and the reason, and make completion a prerequisite of the acknowledgement.
Chase non-completers at 14 and 3 days and escalate to their manager and the policy owner at day 31.
Report completion rates per policy and per population to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee.
checklist.done: each policy has an assigned acknowledgement population with a 30-day due date, training where practice changed, and reported completion rates.

checklist.step: Push flow-down changes into provider contracts
actions: Identify every service provider contract that references or depends on the changed policy — recordkeeper, TPA, custodian, cloud host, actuarial provider.
Raise a contract change request for each, naming the clause to be amended and the effective date, and track it in the contract lifecycle system.
Where the change concerns cybersecurity or data handling, require the provider to confirm compliance in writing and to reflect it in their next independent assessment.
Escalate any provider that will not accept the flow-down to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee as a retention decision under ERISA §404(e).
Record the amendment execution dates against the policy in the inventory.
checklist.done: every affected provider contract has a raised change request tracked to execution, with refusals escalated to the Committee as a retention decision.

checklist.step: Run the exception process for departures from an approved policy
actions: Require any team that cannot comply with an approved policy to raise a GRC policy exception stating the clause, the reason, the compensating control, the exposure and an expiry date no more than 12 months out.
Route ERISA fiduciary policy exceptions to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee for approval, not to a management forum, because the fiduciary duty sits with the Committee.
Refuse any exception with no compensating control or no expiry date; a permanent exception means the policy is wrong and should be changed.
Report the open exception register at every committee sitting with age and exposure.
Close exceptions on evidence that compliance has been restored, and re-test the control before closing.
checklist.done: every departure is a Committee-approved exception with a compensating control, an exposure statement and an expiry date inside 12 months.

checklist.step: Respond out of cycle to a regulatory development
actions: Monitor the DOL EBSA newsroom, Federal Register, Field Assistance Bulletins, Compliance Assistance Releases and litigation outcomes weekly and log anything that changes the standard a policy implements.
Assess within 10 business days whether the development requires a policy change, and if so whether it can wait for the scheduled sitting or must go to the reserved out-of-cycle slot.
Where the change must take effect before the next sitting, prepare a written resolution for the approval body rather than allowing practice to move ahead of the policy.
Notify the affected operating teams the same week with an interim instruction that names the source and the date it takes effect.
Record the development, the assessment and the outcome in the regulatory change log linked to the policy inventory.
checklist.done: each regulatory development is logged, assessed within 10 business days, and resolved by a scheduled change, a written resolution or a recorded no-change decision.

checklist.step: Report policy governance status to the Board annually
actions: Prepare the annual status report: policies in the inventory, approvals completed in the year, any policy that lapsed past 12 months and for how long, out-of-cycle changes, open exceptions with age, and acknowledgement completion rates.
Name each lapsed policy and state the fiduciary exposure assessment General Counsel made for the lapse period, rather than reporting a completion percentage alone.
Set out the coming year's calendar and any policy the Board should expect to change because of a pending regulatory development.
Load the report to the board portal 5 business days before the meeting and have the Corporate Secretary minute the Board's acceptance and directions.
Track the Board's directions on the governance action log to closure.
checklist.done: the annual report is tabled with 5 business days' notice, names every lapsed policy with its exposure assessment, and the Board's acceptance is minuted.

checklist.step: Retain every policy edition and its approval record
actions: File per policy edition: the approved document, the gap assessment memo, the redline and change table, the legal review, the recommendation paper, the approving resolution and minute, and the acknowledgement report.
Apply the 6-year ERISA §107 label from the date the edition ceased to be in force, and the indefinite ERISA §209 label to any policy edition that governed a benefit determination.
Maintain the effective-from and effective-to dates on every edition so it can be shown which policy governed on any given day — this is what an investigator or a court will ask.
Index by policy name, edition, approval body and plan year and confirm the index resolves.
Apply a legal hold suspending disposal where litigation or a DOL investigation touching the policy area is open.
checklist.done: every edition is retained with its full approval record, effective-from and effective-to dates, correct ERISA labels and a resolving index.

testing.step: Rebuild the policy population independently of the inventory
actions: Enumerate every document in the policy library that governs an ERISA plan function, regardless of whether it appears on the inventory.
Add the ERISA duties from the plan documents and the fiduciary register and identify any duty with no governing policy.
Compare both lists to the inventory and list orphan policies in the library and unmapped duties with no policy.
Treat a policy operating outside the inventory as a Critical scope exception, since it is never reviewed and never approved.
Sign the population as complete with the enumeration method, run date and counts.
testing.done: the independently enumerated policy set reconciles to the inventory, with orphan policies and unmapped ERISA duties listed as scope exceptions.

testing.step: Recompute approval currency for every policy in force
actions: For each policy, take the last approval date from the approving minute in the board portal rather than the inventory field.
Recompute months elapsed to plan year end and list every policy past 12 months, with the number of days it has been lapsed.
Confirm the approving minute records a resolution and a vote, not a noting, and that quorum was recorded before the item.
Treat an inventory field that disagrees with the minute as an exception in its own right, since the inventory is what the calendar runs on.
testing.done: each policy's approval currency is recomputed from the approving minute, with lapse days quantified and inventory-to-minute disagreements listed.

testing.step: Draw and document a sample of policy reviews
actions: Take 100% of policies approved in the year that implement a claims, fee-disclosure or cybersecurity obligation, and 100% of out-of-cycle changes.
Take 8 further policy reviews by seeded random selection from the remainder.
Take 100% of open policy exceptions on the GRC register.
Record the seed, population size and selection date so the sample re-draws identically, and confirm the auditor drafted or presented none of the sampled papers.
testing.done: the sample is drawn and reproducible with full coverage of claims, fee, cybersecurity and out-of-cycle policy changes and all open exceptions.

testing.step: Re-perform the gap assessment on a sub-sample
actions: Take 4 sampled policies and read the current eCFR text and EBSA guidance yourself, recording the version dates, without opening the gap assessment memo first.
List the gaps you find and only then compare to the memo; a gap the reviewer missed is an exception even if the policy was approved anyway.
Confirm the memo cites the version dates it relied on — a gap assessment with no stated source version cannot be relied on a year later.
Confirm any Field Assistance Bulletin, Compliance Assistance Release or Advisory Opinion issued since the prior review was considered.
Attach your independent gap list to the workpaper.
testing.done: each sub-sampled policy has an independent gap list compared to the memo, with source version dates verified and missed gaps listed.

testing.step: Trace the approved edition to the published edition
actions: For each sampled policy, take the edition number and effective date from the approving minute and open the edition published in the policy library.
Compare the two documents clause by clause, using a document comparison, and list any difference — post-approval editorial changes are unapproved policy.
Confirm the prior edition is archived with an effective-to date and that no live link still resolves to it.
Recompute the publication interval against the 10-business-day standard from the approval date.
Treat a published edition that differs from the approved one as a Critical exception, not a version-control observation.
testing.done: each sampled policy's published edition matches the minuted edition clause by clause, the prior edition is archived, and the publication interval is recomputed.

testing.step: Test the decision record against the prudence standard
actions: For each sampled approval, confirm the recommendation paper states the decision sought, the options considered and the recommendation, and that the gap assessment and legal review were annexed.
Confirm the paper was on the board portal by the 5-business-day cut-off, using the portal upload timestamp rather than the paper's own date.
Confirm the minute records the options, the discussion, any dissent, the resolution and the vote, and names the edition and effective date.
Treat an approval minuted with no options recorded as failing the ERISA §404(a)(1)(B) evidence standard even where the policy is sound.
testing.done: each sampled approval shows a compliant paper uploaded before the cut-off and a minute recording options, dissent, resolution, vote, edition and effective date.

testing.step: Reconcile acknowledgement and provider flow-down completion
actions: For each sampled policy, take the target population from the role map and compare it to the population actually assigned in the learning management system.
Compute the completion rate against the 95% standard within 30 days of publication and list the non-completers and whether they were escalated.
For policies with provider flow-down, open the contract lifecycle system and confirm each raised change request reached execution, with the amendment date recorded.
Treat an under-assigned population as worse than a low completion rate — the people who never got the task will never show as non-compliant.
testing.done: assigned populations reconcile to the role map, completion is computed against the 95% standard, and every flow-down change request is traced to execution.

testing.step: Test the exception register for compensating controls and expiry
actions: Open every policy exception on the register and confirm it names the clause, the reason, a compensating control, the exposure and an expiry date inside 12 months.
Confirm each ERISA fiduciary exception was approved by the ERISA Plan Administration Committee and traced to a minute, not by a management forum.
Test the compensating control actually operates by inspecting its evidence for the period, rather than accepting its description.
List any exception past expiry, renewed more than once, or lacking an operating compensating control as an exception in the test.
testing.done: every open exception is Committee-approved with a compensating control proved to operate and an unexpired date, or is listed.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise a GRC issue per exception naming the policy, the edition, the control that failed and the fiduciary consequence.

Assign a root cause — policy absent from the inventory, calendar slot missed, gap assessment skipped or undated, edition edited after approval, population under-assigned, flow-down never executed — and a named owner.
Set 30 days for lapsed approvals and published-versus-approved mismatches and 90 days for inventory and process changes, with closure evidence stated up front.
Refer every lapse period to General Counsel for a fiduciary exposure assessment covering decisions taken under the lapsed policy.
Carry every open issue into next year's test as a mandatory retest row.
testing.done: every exception has a GRC issue with root cause, named owner, dated remediation and, for lapses, a counsel exposure assessment.

testing.step: Conclude, obtain independent sign-off and report
actions: Count the zero-tolerance failures — policies in force with no approval inside 12 months, approvals with no documented gap assessment, and published editions differing from the approved edition.
Compute acknowledgement attainment against the 95% standard and the average lapse days across any lapsed policies.
State the conclusion — effective, effective with exceptions, or ineffective — with the workpaper reference behind every figure.
Have the independent reviewer, who owns no policy in the inventory and sits outside the Corporate Secretariat, sign the workpaper.

Report to the Board and the ERISA Plan Administration Committee and file the signed workpaper in the compliance evidence repository under ERISA / Policy Governance / <plan year> with the 6-year label.
testing.done: a signed workpaper counting zero-tolerance failures, stating acknowledgement attainment and a conclusion, is filed with Board reporting dates recorded.

Accountable obligation owner.value: Owns the written information-security program covering ERISA plan systems and participant data — the recordkeeping platform, the claims and appeals platform that runs the 29 CFR 2560.503-1(b) procedures, the participant portal and every provider holding plan data — and reports its status quarterly to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee.

Citation verified against current regula.value: Yes — EBSA Cybersecurity Program Best Practices (2021) and Compliance Assistance Release 2021-01 read against the twelve published practices on dol.gov, ERISA §404(a)(1)(B) prudence as applied to plan data, 29 CFR 2560.503-1(b) written claims procedures the platform must enforce, and 29 CFR 2550.408b-2(c) covered service provider disclosure including the 60-day rule for disclosing changes.

In-scope processes.value: Program governance and role assignment, annual risk assessment, annual independent third-party audit of security controls, access control administration for participant and plan-sponsor data, encryption at rest and in transit, secure SDLC for plan-facing applications, awareness training, business resiliency and incident response, and cloud and service provider security review.

In-scope systems.value: Program document set, control register, risk register, exception register and quarterly attestations held in the GRC platform; identity and access controls administered through the IAM platform and SailPoint IGA; detection and incident evidence in the SIEM/SOAR; vulnerability state in Qualys / Tenable.

Compliance procedure documented.value: ERISA Written Information Security Program — scope statement naming the plans, systems and data elements covered, the twelve EBSA best-practice domains each with named control owners, the annual risk assessment and third-party audit cadence, the access-control and encryption standards, the incident response and resiliency plans, and the provider security review requirements.

Compliance procedure approved.value: Approved by the Chief Info Security Officer and the ERISA Plan Administration Committee, with Board noting; re-approved at least annually and out of cycle whenever EBSA reissues the best practices, a material incident occurs, or a new recordkeeper or cloud provider is onboarded.

Filing/reporting deadlines tracked.value: Annual program review completed within 120 days of plan year end so it can inform the Form 5500 cycle; quarterly control attestations due 20 business days after quarter end; the annual independent controls audit report obtained before the plan's own financial statement audit; provider security changes disclosed to the plan fiduciary no later than 60 days from the date the provider is informed of them under 29 CFR 2550.408b-2(c)(1)(v).

Deadline reminders configured.value: GRC platform reminders to control owners at 20, 10 and 3 days before each quarterly attestation; annual program review milestones at plan year end plus 30, 60, 90 and 120 days; contract-anniversary alerts 90 days before each provider's SOC 2 report period ends so a bridge letter is requested in time.

Evidence retained per the retention requ.value: Program document editions, risk assessments, third-party audit reports, control attestations, access reviews, encryption inventories, training records, incident records and provider assessments retained 6 years per ERISA §107, with incident records touching a participant's benefit entitlement kept per ERISA §209.

Violations/exceptions logged with dispos.value: Missed attestations, controls without owners, unencrypted participant data stores, overdue access reviews, providers without a current independent assessment and any best-practice domain with no evidence are logged with owner, exposure, compensating control and a dated remediation.

Remediation sign-off captured.value: Signs off closure of every program gap and personally approves any risk acceptance, which must then be ratified by the ERISA Plan Administration Committee because the fiduciary duty over plan data sits with the plan fiduciary, not with technology.

Test population (in-scope transactions,.value: The twelve EBSA best-practice domains with their control register entries, all systems and data stores holding ERISA participant data, all privileged and standard access to those systems, all providers with access to plan data, and all incidents affecting participant data in the period.

Pass/fail thresholds.value: Every one of the twelve EBSA best-practice domains must have a named owner, a documented control and current evidence — any domain with no evidence is a fail; zero tolerance for unencrypted participant data at rest or in transit, for a provider holding plan data with no current independent assessment, and for privileged access without a completed review in the last quarter.

Compliance test frequency matched to the.value: The program is reviewed annually and attested quarterly; control testing runs quarterly on access, encryption and incident controls, with the full twelve-domain assessment performed annually within 120 days of plan year end.

Independent reviewer (segregated from th.value: Reviewer must sit outside the CISO organisation and own no control in the register; the annual independent controls audit is performed by an external firm engaged by the ERISA Plan Administration Committee.

Evidence location for test results.value: Quarterly and annual WISP test workpapers — domain coverage matrix, control test results, access review reconciliation, encryption inventory, provider assessment register and exception schedule — in the compliance evidence repository under ERISA / Cybersecurity / <period>.

Regulator-ready documentation.value: Program pack mapped explicitly to the twelve EBSA Cybersecurity Program Best Practices with the evidence reference for each, plus the latest risk assessment, independent audit report and incident summary, producible to an EBSA investigator or a plan sponsor's fiduciary within 10 business days.

Regulator response path.value: Chief Info Security Officer prepares the technical response; General Counsel is the single channel to EBSA and to plan sponsors on any incident affecting participant data, and decides on breach notification obligations with the Privacy Officer.

checklist.step: Define the program scope in plan and data terms
actions: Name in the program document every ERISA plan covered, with plan number and sponsor, and every system holding participant data — recordkeeping platform, claims and appeals platform, participant portal, payroll and contribution interfaces, document repository and data warehouse.
Define the data elements in scope: name, Social Security number, date of birth, compensation, account balance, beneficiary designations, health claim data and bank details.
Trace the data flow from payroll through the recordkeeper to the participant portal and out to each provider, and record every place plan data comes to rest.
Have the Data Governance Lead confirm the inventory against the data catalogue so shadow copies in reporting extracts and test environments are captured.
Get the ERISA Plan Administration Committee to approve the scope statement, since a scope that omits a system omits the duty.
checklist.done: the program document names every covered plan, system, provider and data element, traced against the data catalogue and approved by the Committee.

checklist.step: Map the program to the twelve EBSA best practices with named owners
actions: Create one control register domain per EBSA best practice: formal documented program, annual risk assessment, reliable annual third-party audit, clearly defined security roles, strong access controls, third-party and cloud security reviews, awareness training, secure SDLC, business resiliency, encryption in transit and at rest, strong technical controls, and appropriate response to past incidents.
Attach to each domain the controls that implement it, the evidence each control produces, its frequency, and a single named owner with a deputy.
Reject any domain whose only evidence is the policy document itself — a policy is not evidence that the control operates.
Flag domains with no control or no owner to the Chief Info Security Officer within 5 business days of the mapping.
Publish the domain-to-control matrix so the program can be shown to a regulator in the regulator's own structure.
checklist.done: all twelve EBSA domains have controls, named owners, deputies and defined evidence in the GRC control register, with unowned domains escalated.

checklist.step: Assign and evidence the security roles the program depends on
actions: Document the security organisation for plan data: who owns program governance, access administration, detection and response, vulnerability management, third-party assessment and resiliency.
Confirm each named role has the authority and the budget to act, and record the reporting line into the Chief Info Security Officer and up to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee.
Confirm segregation between those who grant access and those who review it, and between those who develop plan-facing applications and those who release them.
Record each role holder's relevant qualification and the training they completed in the year.
Refresh the role assignment whenever a role holder changes and record the effective dates so any control failure can be tied to an accountable person.
checklist.done: every program role has a named holder with authority, reporting line, segregation from conflicting duties and dated effective periods.

checklist.step: Enforce access control over participant data
actions: Define entitlements over plan systems by role and enforce least privilege, with separate entitlements for read, transact and administer.
Require multi-factor authentication for every internal user of a plan system and for participant access to the portal, and record the enrolment rate.
Vault and session-record every privileged account on the recordkeeping and claims platforms through CyberArk, and prohibit shared administrator credentials.
Run quarterly access recertification in SailPoint IGA, requiring the business owner to confirm each entitlement, and auto-revoke anything not recertified inside 15 days of the campaign closing.
Wire joiner-mover-leaver events from the HRIS so access is removed on the leaving date, and reconcile leavers to revocations weekly.
checklist.done: least-privilege entitlements, universal MFA, vaulted privileged access and a quarterly recertification with auto-revocation are all evidenced, with leaver revocations reconciled weekly.

checklist.step: Encrypt participant data at rest and in transit and prove it
actions: Build an encryption inventory listing every store holding participant data — databases, file shares, backups, object storage, laptops and the data warehouse — with the encryption method and key management for each.
Enforce TLS 1.2 or above on every interface carrying participant data, including the payroll-to-recordkeeper feed and any provider SFTP, and disable legacy protocols and ciphers.
Confirm keys are managed in a key management service with rotation, split knowledge and audit logging, and that no key material sits in application configuration.
Scan for unencrypted participant data outside sanctioned stores — extracts on file shares, test environments seeded with production data — and remediate or tokenise what is found.
Re-run the inventory and the scan quarterly and attach the output as the domain's evidence.
checklist.done: an encryption inventory covers every participant-data store and interface with method and key management recorded, and the quarterly unencrypted-data scan is clean or remediated.

checklist.step: Run the secure development lifecycle for plan-facing applications
actions: Require threat modelling for any change to the participant portal, the claims and appeals workflow or the recordkeeping interfaces, and record the model with the change.
Gate the pipeline on static analysis in SonarQube, dependency scanning and secrets detection, and block the release on a critical finding rather than warning.
Require security testing before release for changes touching authentication, entitlements, payment instructions or beneficiary data.
Prohibit production participant data in development and test environments, and enforce masking at the data-provisioning step.
Confirm the claims and appeals workflow enforces the 29 CFR 2560.503-1 timing and reviewer-independence rules in code, so a control break cannot be introduced by configuration.
checklist.done: plan-facing changes carry a threat model, pass blocking pipeline gates, use masked non-production data, and the claims workflow's regulatory timing and independence rules are enforced in code.

checklist.step: Maintain incident response for participant-data events
actions: Maintain a plan-data incident playbook covering account takeover, phishing against participants, provider breach, ransomware on a plan system and insider misuse.
Define severity by participants affected and data sensitivity, with mandatory notification of the ERISA Plan Administration Committee, the plan sponsor and General Counsel at the defined thresholds.
Wire detections for the plan-specific patterns — bulk statement downloads, distribution requests following an email change, and logins from unusual geographies against dormant accounts.
Run a tabletop exercise at least annually using a participant-data scenario with the plan committee present, not only the technology teams, and record the findings and actions.
Close every incident with a post-incident review naming the control that failed and the change that prevents recurrence, since EBSA expects a demonstrated response to past incidents.
checklist.done: a plan-data playbook with severity thresholds, tuned detections, an annual committee-attended tabletop and post-incident reviews naming failed controls are all in place.

checklist.step: Prove business resiliency for plan administration
actions: Set recovery time and recovery point objectives for each plan system based on what participants lose if it is down — contribution posting, distribution processing, claim adjudication deadlines under 29 CFR 2560.503-1.
Confirm backups of participant data are taken, encrypted, held offline or immutable, and restorable, and test a full restore of the recordkeeping data at least annually.
Test failover of the participant portal and the claims platform and record the achieved recovery times against the objectives.
Confirm the recordkeeper and other critical providers have tested resiliency plans and obtain their most recent test results.
Report achieved versus target recovery times to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee annually.
checklist.done: recovery objectives are set per plan system, a restore and a failover test are completed with achieved times recorded, and provider test results are on file.

checklist.step: Review the security of every provider holding plan data
actions: Maintain the register of providers with access to plan data — recordkeeper, TPA, custodian, print and mail vendor, cloud hosts, analytics providers — with the data elements each holds.

Obtain and read each provider's SOC 2 Type II report annually, checking the period covered, the exceptions noted and the complementary user entity controls the plan must operate, and obtain a bridge letter for any gap to today.
Assess against the EBSA expectation of an independent security assessment: a self-attested questionnaire alone does not satisfy it for a provider holding participant data.
Confirm the contract carries the security, breach notification, audit right, subcontractor and data return clauses, and require change disclosures within the 29 CFR 2550.408b-2(c) 60-day rule.
Escalate any provider with no current independent assessment to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee as a retention decision under ERISA §404(e).
checklist.done: every provider holding plan data has a current independent assessment read and documented, complementary user controls identified, and contract clauses confirmed.

checklist.step: Deliver awareness training targeted at plan data risks
actions: Assign annual security awareness training to everyone with access to participant data, with a module specific to plan data — social engineering aimed at distribution requests, beneficiary changes and address changes.
Assign a separate module to contact centre agents covering identity proofing before any account change, since the call centre is the usual route into an account takeover.
Run phishing simulations at least quarterly against the plan operations and contact centre populations and record click and report rates.
Chase non-completers at 14 and 3 days before the due date and escalate to their manager and the control owner after it.
Report completion and simulation results to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee as evidence of the EBSA training practice.
checklist.done: everyone with participant-data access has completed targeted annual training, quarterly phishing simulations are run and results are reported to the Committee.

checklist.step: Attest the control register quarterly
actions: Launch the quarterly attestation to every control owner 20 business days before the due date, requiring them to confirm the control operated and to attach the period's evidence.
Reject any attestation with no evidence attached; an owner's assertion is not evidence and will not survive an EBSA request.
Record every control that did not operate as a gap with an exposure statement and a compensating control, not as a late attestation.
Compute the domain coverage position — the twelve domains, the controls attested, the gaps open — and publish it inside 20 business days of quarter end.
Escalate any domain with no evidence for the quarter to the Chief Info Security Officer the day the window closes.
checklist.done: quarterly attestations are complete with evidence attached, gaps recorded with compensating controls, and domain coverage published within 20 business days of quarter end.

checklist.step: Run the annual program review within 120 days of plan year end
actions: Reassess the program against the current EBSA best practices text and against the year's risk assessment, incidents, audit findings and provider assessments.
Update the scope for new plans, new systems, new providers and any change of recordkeeper, since scope drift is the usual cause of an uncovered system.
Redline the program document, record what changed and why, and identify any control that must change with an owner and a date.
Complete the review within 120 days of plan year end so the outcome is available for the Form 5500 cycle and the plan's financial statement audit.
Take the reviewed program to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee for approval and have the approval minuted.
checklist.done: the program is reassessed against current EBSA text and the year's evidence, redlined with reasons, and Committee-approved within 120 days of plan year end.

checklist.step: Obtain the annual independent audit of security controls
actions: Engage an external firm, appointed by the ERISA Plan Administration Committee rather than by the CISO organisation, to audit the security controls over plan data.
Agree a scope that covers the twelve EBSA domains and names the systems, and require the report to state the testing performed rather than only the conclusion.
Read the findings, agree a remediation plan with owners and dates, and load every finding into the GRC platform as an issue.
Give the report to the plan's independent qualified public accountant and to any plan sponsor that requests it under its own fiduciary duty.
Confirm the audit is obtained before the plan's financial statement audit so the findings inform it.
checklist.done: a Committee-engaged external firm has audited the twelve domains, findings are loaded as GRC issues with owners and dates, and the report is available before the plan audit.

checklist.step: Report the program status to the plan committee quarterly
actions: Prepare the quarterly paper: domain coverage against the twelve practices, attestation completion, open gaps with exposure and age, access recertification results, encryption scan results, incidents affecting participant data, provider assessment status and training and phishing results.
Present risk in participant terms — how many participants' data is exposed by each open gap — rather than in control-language only.
Bring every proposed risk acceptance to the Committee for ratification, because the fiduciary duty over plan data cannot be accepted away by technology management.
Load the paper to the board portal 5 business days before the sitting and have the Corporate Secretary minute the decisions.
Track Committee actions on the governance action log to closure.
checklist.done: the quarterly paper covers all twelve domains in participant-impact terms, every risk acceptance is Committee-ratified, and decisions are minuted.

checklist.step: Retain the program evidence for the ERISA period
actions: Export each program edition, risk assessment, independent audit report, quarterly attestation pack, access recertification result, encryption inventory, training record, incident record and provider assessment to the compliance evidence repository under ERISA / Cybersecurity / <period>.
Apply the 6-year ERISA §107 retention label and the indefinite ERISA §209 label to any incident record touching a participant's benefit entitlement.
Maintain effective-from and effective-to dates on every program edition so it can be shown which program was in force on the date of any incident.
Index by domain, control, plan and period so an EBSA request can be answered in the regulator's own structure within 10 business days.
Apply legal holds suspending disposal where an incident, a DOL investigation or litigation touching plan data is open.
checklist.done: all program evidence is retained with ERISA labels, effective-date ranges per edition, and an index organised by EBSA domain, control, plan and period.

testing.step: Build the population of covered systems, providers and controls
actions: Extract the control register with its twelve-domain mapping, owners, frequencies and evidence definitions.
Independently enumerate systems holding participant data from the CMDB, the data catalogue and the provider register, and compare to the program scope statement.
List every system or provider holding plan data that is absent from the program scope — an uncovered system is the failure that matters most.
Reconcile the control register to the twelve EBSA practices and list any domain with no control or no owner.
Sign the population as complete with the extract queries, run date and counts.
testing.done: the enumerated systems and providers reconcile to the program scope and every EBSA domain maps to at least one owned control, or the gaps are listed.

testing.step: Reconcile the program document to the current EBSA text
actions: Open the EBSA Cybersecurity Program Best Practices page on dol.gov and Compliance Assistance Release 2021-01 and record the version and date read.
Compare each of the twelve practices to the program document and confirm the document addresses it in substance, not by restating the heading.
Confirm the annual review was completed within 120 days of plan year end by taking the approval date from the Committee minute rather than the document footer.
List any practice the program document addresses only by reference to another policy that does not in fact contain it.
testing.done: each of the twelve practices is traced to substantive program text, and the annual review date is verified from the approving Committee minute.

testing.step: Draw a documented sample of controls and access records
actions: Take at least one control from each of the twelve domains, and 100% of controls whose failure would expose participant data directly — access recertification, MFA enforcement, encryption, privileged access, provider assessment.
Take 30 user entitlements over the recordkeeping and claims platforms by seeded random selection, plus 100% of privileged accounts.
Take 100% of providers holding participant data and 100% of incidents affecting participant data in the period.
Record the seed, population sizes and selection date so the sample re-draws identically, and confirm the auditor owns none of the sampled controls.
testing.done: the sample covers every domain, all direct-exposure controls, all privileged accounts, all providers and all incidents, and is reproducible from the recorded seed.

testing.step: Re-perform the access recertification on the sampled entitlements
actions: For each sampled entitlement, confirm a recertification decision exists for the current quarter and that the reviewer was the business owner, not the entitlement holder or their delegate.
Compare the entitlement to the role definition and identify access beyond least privilege, particularly transact and administer rights held by read-only roles.
Reconcile the leaver list from the HRIS to revocation timestamps and compute days from leaving date to revocation for every leaver in the period.
Confirm entitlements not recertified within 15 days of campaign close were actually auto-revoked, by checking the account state rather than the campaign status.
Confirm every privileged account is vaulted with session recording and that no shared administrator credential exists on the plan systems.
testing.done: each sampled entitlement has an owner recertification, leaver revocation days are computed from HRIS source, and auto-revocation and privileged vaulting are verified in the account state.

testing.step: Verify encryption coverage independently of the inventory
actions: Take 10 data stores from the enumerated system list and inspect the actual encryption configuration rather than the inventory entry.
Test the transport configuration of the payroll-to-recordkeeper feed, the provider SFTP endpoints and the participant portal, confirming TLS 1.2 or above and that legacy ciphers are refused.
Confirm key management uses a key management service with rotation and audit logging, and search application configuration and source repositories for embedded key material.
Re-run the unencrypted-participant-data scan across file shares and non-production environments and compare the result to the control owner's reported result.
Treat any participant data found unencrypted, or production data found in a test environment, as a Critical exception.
testing.done: encryption is verified from live configuration on sampled stores and interfaces, key material is confirmed absent from code and config, and the independent scan is compared to the owner's result.

testing.step: Re-read the provider assessments and the user-entity controls
actions: Open each provider's SOC 2 Type II report and check the period covered ends no earlier than the plan year end less the bridge letter coverage, and read the exceptions section rather than the opinion alone.
List the complementary user entity controls the report assumes and confirm each is implemented on the plan side with evidence — an unimplemented user-entity control voids the reliance.
Confirm the contract carries breach notification, audit right, subcontractor and data return clauses and the 29 CFR 2550.408b-2(c) 60-day change disclosure obligation.
Confirm any change the provider disclosed in the period was disclosed within 60 days of the date the provider was informed of it.
Treat any provider holding participant data with no independent assessment as a Critical ERISA §404(e) monitoring failure.
testing.done: each provider's report period, exceptions and complementary user controls are verified with plan-side evidence, and the 60-day change disclosure rule is tested.

testing.step: Re-perform the incident handling test on participant-data events
actions: For each incident affecting participant data, recompute detection-to-containment and containment-to-notification intervals from raw log and ticket timestamps.
Confirm the severity assigned matches the participants affected and the data sensitivity, and that the Committee, the plan sponsor and General Counsel were notified at the defined thresholds.
Confirm a post-incident review exists that names the failed control and a change, and trace that change to an implemented control state rather than a planned action.
Confirm the annual tabletop happened with plan committee attendance and that its findings became tracked actions.
Treat an incident closed with no named failed control as failing the EBSA past-incident response practice.
testing.done: each incident has recomputed intervals, verified threshold notifications and a post-incident review whose remediation is traced to an implemented control.

testing.step: Test attestation quality and domain evidence coverage
actions: Open each quarterly attestation for the sampled controls and confirm evidence is attached and that the evidence covers the attested period, not an earlier one.
Inspect the evidence itself for at least one control per domain and judge whether it actually demonstrates the control operated.
Compute attestation completion and on-time rates against the 20-business-day standard.
List any domain with an attestation but no substantive evidence as a fail against the zero-tolerance domain-evidence threshold.
testing.done: each sampled attestation has period-correct evidence inspected for substance, completion and timeliness are computed, and evidence-free domains are listed as fails.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise a GRC issue per exception naming the EBSA domain, the control, the system or provider and the number of participants exposed.

Assign a root cause — system outside program scope, domain with no owner, entitlement recertified by the holder, leaver revocation not wired to the HRIS, store missing from the encryption inventory, provider assessment expired, user-entity control never implemented — and a named owner.
Set 30 days for access, encryption and provider exceptions and 90 days for architectural changes, with the closure evidence stated when the issue is raised.
Route every proposed risk acceptance to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee for ratification rather than closing it within technology.
Carry every open issue into the next quarterly test as a mandatory retest row.
testing.done: every exception has a GRC issue naming its EBSA domain and exposed participant count, a root cause, a named owner and a dated remediation.

testing.step: Conclude, obtain independent sign-off and report
actions: Count the zero-tolerance failures — any of the twelve domains with no evidence, unencrypted participant data, a provider with no current independent assessment, and privileged access without a completed quarterly review.
Compute domain coverage, attestation completion and access recertification attainment, and state the conclusion — effective, effective with exceptions, or ineffective.
Have the independent reviewer, who sits outside the CISO organisation and owns no control in the register, sign the workpaper.
Report the conclusion, the exception schedule and any participant-data incident to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee and the Audit Committee.
File the signed workpaper in the compliance evidence repository under ERISA / Cybersecurity / <period> with the 6-year ERISA §107 label.
testing.done: a signed workpaper counting zero-tolerance failures by EBSA domain, stating coverage rates and a conclusion, is filed with Committee reporting dates.

Accountable obligation owner.value: Owns the annual cybersecurity risk assessment over ERISA plan systems and participant data required by the second EBSA best practice, and owns remediation of its findings to closure; the assessment scope and the residual-risk decisions are ratified by the ERISA Plan Administration Committee.

Citation verified against current regula.value: Yes — EBSA Cybersecurity Program Best Practices (2021), which call for a prudent annual risk assessment and remediation of identified weaknesses, and Compliance Assistance Release 2021-01, read on dol.gov at assessment planning, together with ERISA §404(a)(1)(B) prudence and §404(e) prudent selection and monitoring as applied to providers holding participant data.

In-scope processes.value: Asset and data-flow identification for plan systems, threat and scenario development, control effectiveness testing including penetration testing and vulnerability scanning, inherent and residual risk scoring, provider and cloud risk assessment, findings remediation tracking, retest and closure, and reporting to the plan fiduciary.

In-scope systems.value: Risk register, assessment workpapers, scoring and findings tracked in the GRC platform; technical evidence drawn from Qualys / Tenable for vulnerability state, CrowdStrike Falcon for endpoint coverage, Splunk SIEM for detection coverage and SailPoint IGA for entitlement data; remediation work managed as tickets in the ITSM/security ticketing system.

Compliance procedure documented.value: ERISA Cybersecurity Risk Assessment Methodology — scope rule tying assessment to plan systems and participant data, the threat catalogue, the likelihood and impact scales expressed in participants affected and benefit disruption, control effectiveness rating rules, residual risk tolerance, the finding severity matrix with fixed remediation windows, and the retest-before-closure rule.

Compliance procedure approved.value: Methodology approved by the Chief Info Security Officer and the Chief Risk Officer and ratified by the ERISA Plan Administration Committee; re-approved annually and out of cycle after any material incident or any change of recordkeeper or hosting arrangement.

Filing/reporting deadlines tracked.value: Annual: scope agreed within 30 days of plan year end, fieldwork complete within 90 days, the assessment report issued and Committee-approved within 120 days of plan year end; findings remediated to fixed windows — Critical 30 days, High 60 days, Medium 90 days, Low at the next annual cycle — with retest before closure and a re-assessment triggered within 30 days of any material incident or provider change.

Deadline reminders configured.value: GRC platform reminders against the 30/90/120-day assessment milestones; per-finding reminders to the remediation owner at 75%, 90% and 100% of the severity window elapsed, escalating to the Chief Info Security Officer on the due date and to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee at due date plus 15 days.

Evidence retained per the retention requ.value: Scope statement, asset and data-flow inventory, threat catalogue, control test evidence, penetration test and scan reports, scoring workpapers, the assessment report, the findings register and retest evidence, retained 6 years per ERISA §107 with technical exploit detail held under restricted access.

Violations/exceptions logged with dispos.value: Findings past their severity window, findings closed without a retest, systems excluded from scope without a documented basis and risk acceptances not ratified by the plan committee are logged with owner, exposure and a dated resolution.

Remediation sign-off captured.value: Signs closure of every Critical and High finding on retest evidence, and every risk acceptance, which the ERISA Plan Administration Committee must then ratify because residual risk to participant data is a fiduciary decision.

Test population (in-scope transactions,.value: Every plan system and participant data store in the assessment scope, every provider and cloud service holding participant data, all findings raised by the annual assessment, the penetration tests and the vulnerability scans in the year, and all findings carried forward from the prior assessment.

Pass/fail thresholds.value: Zero tolerance — any plan system or participant data store excluded from scope without a documented, approved basis; any Critical finding open past 30 days or High past 60 days; any finding closed without retest evidence; and any risk acceptance not ratified by the ERISA Plan Administration Committee.

Compliance test frequency matched to the.value: The assessment is annual; the verification test runs annually over the completed assessment within 60 days of the report, with a quarterly interim test of the findings register ageing and closure quality.

Independent reviewer (segregated from th.value: Reviewer must sit outside the CISO organisation, must not have performed any part of the assessment, and must not own any finding in the register.

Evidence location for test results.value: Annual risk assessment verification workpaper — scope reconciliation, threat and scenario coverage matrix, scoring re-performance, findings ageing recomputation, retest evidence inspection and exception schedule — in the compliance evidence repository under ERISA / Cyber Risk Assessment / <plan year>.

Regulator-ready documentation.value: Assessment report with scope, methodology, findings by severity, residual risk position and the remediation status at report date, plus the findings register and retest evidence, producible to an EBSA investigator or a plan sponsor within 10 business days, with exploit detail redacted.

Regulator response path.value: Chief Info Security Officer prepares the technical narrative; General Counsel is the single channel to EBSA and to plan sponsors, and decides with the Privacy Officer on any disclosure obligation arising from a finding that indicates prior participant-data exposure.

checklist.step: Agree the assessment scope in plan terms within 30 days of plan year end
actions: List the plans, systems, data stores, interfaces and providers to be assessed, drawn from the written information-security program scope statement and the data catalogue.

Include the participant portal, the recordkeeping platform, the claims and appeals platform, the payroll-to-recordkeeper interface, the print and mail vendor pipeline and every cloud service holding participant data.
Record and justify any exclusion in writing with an expiry date; an undocumented exclusion is the most common reason an assessment fails to satisfy the EBSA practice.
Confirm scope changes since last year — new plans taken on, a pension risk transfer transaction, a recordkeeper migration, a new analytics platform.
Have the ERISA Plan Administration Committee approve the scope and minute the approval before fieldwork starts.
checklist.done: a Committee-approved scope statement lists every plan system, store, interface and provider assessed, with each exclusion justified and dated.

checklist.step: Refresh the asset and data-flow inventory the assessment rests on
actions: Reconcile the plan system list to the CMDB and the data catalogue and confirm each entry has an owner, a hosting model and a data classification.

Map participant data flows end to end: payroll contribution files in, recordkeeper processing, portal presentation, statement print, claims adjudication, data warehouse extracts and provider transfers out.
Identify every copy — reporting extracts, non-production environments, backups, provider-held copies — because an assessment that only covers the system of record understates exposure.
Record the participant counts and the data elements held in each store, so impact can be expressed in participants affected.
Sign the inventory as the assessment baseline and freeze it for the fieldwork period.
checklist.done: a signed, frozen inventory maps every participant data store and flow with owner, hosting model, data elements and participant counts.

checklist.step: Build the threat catalogue and the plan-specific scenarios
actions: Assemble the threat catalogue from current threat intelligence, the sector's incident history, the organisation's own incidents and near misses, and the EBSA best-practice themes.

Write plan-specific scenarios rather than generic ones: participant account takeover leading to a fraudulent distribution, phishing of a plan operations user with bulk data access, ransomware on the recordkeeping platform during a contribution cycle, breach at the print and mail vendor, insider export of beneficiary and Social Security data.
For each scenario name the assets touched, the attack path through the mapped data flows, and the participants affected if it succeeds.
Have the SOC Lead confirm each scenario against actual detection coverage in Splunk SIEM so the assessment tests reality rather than design.
Review the catalogue with the Chief Risk Officer so the plan scenarios line up with the enterprise operational risk taxonomy.
checklist.done: each scenario names its assets, attack path, participant impact and detection coverage, and the catalogue is reviewed against enterprise risk taxonomy.

checklist.step: Score inherent risk in participant terms
actions: Score likelihood from threat intelligence, exposure of the asset and the organisation's own incident history, using the methodology's fixed scale rather than a workshop opinion.

Score impact on the participant-facing scale: participants whose data is exposed, benefit payments delayed or misdirected, statutory claim deadlines missed under 29 CFR 2560.503-1, and plan asset loss.
Record the reasoning and the data behind every score in the GRC risk register, since a score with no reasoning is not evidence of a prudent assessment.
Have a second assessor challenge each score above the tolerance line and record the challenge and its outcome.
Publish the inherent risk position before control testing so control effectiveness can be measured against it.
checklist.done: each scenario has a reasoned inherent likelihood and participant-impact score in the risk register, challenged where above tolerance.

checklist.step: Test the controls that stand between the threat and the participant
actions: For each scenario, list the preventive, detective and responsive controls on the attack path and test each rather than accepting its design description.
Test authentication and identity proofing on the participant portal and in the contact centre, including the controls on email, address and bank-detail changes that precede a fraudulent distribution.
Test entitlement boundaries by attempting cross-account and cross-plan data access with a standard user entitlement in a controlled environment.
Test detection by confirming the SIEM rules for bulk export, distribution-after-contact-change and dormant-account login actually fire, using controlled test events.
Record for each control the test performed, the evidence and an effectiveness rating, and file the evidence in the assessment workpaper.
checklist.done: every control on each scenario's attack path has a performed test, filed evidence and an effectiveness rating.

checklist.step: Run the technical vulnerability position across plan systems
actions: Run authenticated scans across every in-scope plan system, including the participant portal, the recordkeeping and claims platform hosts and the interface servers.
Reconcile scan coverage to the asset inventory and investigate every asset with no scan result — unscanned assets are the ones that carry the unknown exposure.
Confirm endpoint agent coverage in CrowdStrike Falcon for every workstation with access to participant data and list the uncovered ones.
Age the open vulnerabilities against the organisation's remediation standard and extract the Critical and High set on internet-facing plan systems for the assessment.
Attach the coverage reconciliation and the aged vulnerability extract to the assessment workpaper.
checklist.done: authenticated scan coverage is reconciled to the asset inventory with gaps listed, endpoint coverage is confirmed, and an aged Critical/High extract is filed.

checklist.step: Commission penetration testing against the participant-facing path
actions: Scope an external test of the participant portal and its authentication, session management, account recovery and transaction authorisation, and an internal test of lateral movement toward the recordkeeping data.
Include a social engineering component against plan operations and the contact centre, targeting the identity-proofing controls that guard distributions and beneficiary changes.
Require the tester to demonstrate impact in participant terms — what data could be read, what transaction could be initiated — rather than reporting findings by CVSS alone.
Agree rules of engagement, test windows and a data-handling agreement so no live participant data leaves the environment.
Load every finding into the GRC platform against the scenario it proves and attach the tester's evidence.
checklist.done: external, internal and social-engineering testing is completed under agreed rules with findings demonstrating participant impact loaded against their scenarios.

checklist.step: Assess the providers and cloud services separately
actions: For each provider holding participant data, read the current SOC 2 Type II report and any ISO 27001 certificate, note the exceptions and the complementary user entity controls, and score the residual provider risk.

Where the provider is a cloud host, assess the configuration the organisation owns — storage exposure, key management, network boundaries, logging — because the shared responsibility model leaves those with the plan fiduciary.
Exercise the contractual audit right or issue a targeted questionnaire where the report does not cover a material scenario, and record the response.
Score provider concentration: a single recordkeeper failure that would stop contribution posting and distributions for every plan is a plan-level risk, not a vendor issue.
Feed the provider scores into the assessment as their own risk lines rather than folding them into an internal control rating.
checklist.done: every provider and cloud service has a scored residual risk line supported by a current independent report, an owned-configuration assessment and a concentration view.

checklist.step: Compute residual risk and test it against tolerance
actions: Apply the tested control effectiveness ratings to the inherent scores using the methodology's rules to derive residual risk per scenario.
Compare each residual score to the tolerance the ERISA Plan Administration Committee set and list every scenario above it.
Show the movement from the prior year assessment per scenario and explain each change by the control that improved or degraded, not by a re-scoring judgement.
Where residual risk is above tolerance and cannot be remediated within the severity window, prepare a formal risk acceptance with exposure in participants affected and an expiry date.
Record the whole computation in the risk register so it can be re-performed by a reviewer.
checklist.done: each scenario has a residual score derived from tested control effectiveness, compared to Committee tolerance, with year-on-year movement explained by control changes.

checklist.step: Raise findings with fixed severity windows and named owners
actions: Raise one finding per control weakness with the scenario it exposes, the participants affected, the evidence and the recommended remediation.
Assign severity from the matrix and set the due date automatically: Critical 30 days, High 60 days, Medium 90 days, Low at the next annual cycle.
Name a single accountable owner in the team that operates the control, and record their written acceptance of the finding and the date.
State the closure evidence required at the point of raising — a configuration state, a rerun scan result, a retest report — so closure cannot later be argued.
Link every finding to the scenario and to the EBSA best-practice domain it belongs to, so remediation progress can be reported in the regulator's structure.
checklist.done: each finding carries severity, an automatic due date, a named accepting owner, pre-stated closure evidence and links to its scenario and EBSA domain.

checklist.step: Issue the assessment report within 120 days of plan year end
actions: Write the report with scope and exclusions, methodology, scenarios tested, control effectiveness, findings by severity, residual risk against tolerance and the movement since last year.
State the participant exposure of each above-tolerance scenario in plain numbers rather than in heat-map colours.
Include the remediation plan with owners and dates and the risk acceptances being proposed.
Issue within 120 days of plan year end so the result is available for the plan's financial statement audit and the Form 5500 cycle.
Redact exploit detail from the distributed version and keep the full technical annex under restricted access.
checklist.done: the report issues within 120 days with scope, methodology, findings by severity, participant exposure, remediation plan and proposed acceptances, with exploit detail restricted.

checklist.step: Obtain plan committee ratification of residual risk
actions: Table the report to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee with the decisions sought clearly stated: accept the residual position, approve the remediation plan, ratify each risk acceptance.
Present each proposed risk acceptance individually with participants exposed, the compensating control and the expiry date; a bundled acceptance is not a fiduciary decision.
Load the paper to the board portal 5 business days ahead and have the Corporate Secretary minute the discussion, dissent, resolutions and votes.
Where the Committee declines an acceptance, record the funding or timing decision it makes instead and the new owner and date.
Publish the ratified position back into the risk register within 5 business days of the meeting.
checklist.done: the Committee has ratified or rejected each residual risk and acceptance individually, with the decisions minuted and reflected in the risk register.

checklist.step: Drive remediation to the severity windows
actions: Work findings in severity order, tracking each as a ticket with the closure evidence field populated before the ticket can move to Resolved.
Report ageing weekly to the Chief Info Security Officer showing findings at 75%, 90% and 100% of their window elapsed.
Escalate any Critical finding at day 25 and any High at day 50 to the accountable owner's director, and to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee at due date plus 15 days.
Refuse date extensions without a fresh exposure assessment and a compensating control, and record every extension with the approver.
Where a fix requires a provider change, raise it into the provider's own remediation process and track it through the vendor scorecard rather than closing it internally.
checklist.done: findings are worked in severity order with weekly ageing reporting, defined escalations and every extension supported by a fresh exposure assessment.

checklist.step: Retest before closing any finding
actions: Re-perform the original test that raised each finding rather than reviewing the owner's change record.
For vulnerability findings, re-run the authenticated scan and confirm the finding no longer returns on the affected assets rather than on a sample.
For control findings, re-execute the control test — attempt the cross-account access, replay the detection test event, re-check the configuration state.
For penetration test findings, obtain a retest from the original tester where the finding demonstrated participant impact.
Attach the retest evidence to the finding and close only on that evidence, with the Chief Info Security Officer signing every Critical and High closure.
checklist.done: every closed finding carries retest evidence from a re-performed test, with Critical and High closures signed by the Chief Info Security Officer.

checklist.step: Re-assess out of cycle after an incident or a material change
actions: Trigger a targeted re-assessment within 30 days of any material participant-data incident, any recordkeeper or hosting change, or any provider breach affecting plan data.
Scope the re-assessment to the scenarios and controls the event touches rather than repeating the full annual exercise.
Feed the post-incident review's named failed control straight into the risk register as a control effectiveness downgrade, so residual risk moves with reality.
Report the re-assessment result to the ERISA Plan Administration Committee at its next sitting or sooner where the residual position moved above tolerance.
Record the trigger, the scope and the outcome in the assessment log so the annual report can show the year's full assessment activity.
checklist.done: each qualifying event triggers a scoped re-assessment within 30 days whose result updates the risk register and is reported to the Committee.

testing.step: Reconcile the assessment scope to the real estate holding participant data
actions: Enumerate systems and data stores holding participant data independently from the CMDB, the data catalogue, the provider register and the network asset inventory.
Compare to the Committee-approved scope statement and list every asset or provider absent from scope.
For each documented exclusion, test whether the stated basis still holds and whether the expiry date has passed.
Treat any in-scope-by-fact asset excluded without an approved basis as a Critical exception, since an unassessed system carries unmeasured participant exposure.
Sign the population as complete with the enumeration sources, run date and counts.
testing.done: the independently enumerated estate reconciles to the approved scope, with every unapproved exclusion raised as a Critical exception.

testing.step: Reconcile the assessment to the methodology it claims to follow
actions: Read the approved methodology and confirm the assessment used its scales, its control effectiveness rules and its severity matrix rather than an ad hoc approach.
Confirm the impact scale was expressed in participants affected and benefit disruption, not in generic financial bands, since the fiduciary duty runs to participants.
Confirm the methodology itself was re-approved in the year and ratified by the ERISA Plan Administration Committee.
List any scenario scored outside the methodology as a methodology exception separate from the risk it describes.
testing.done: the assessment is confirmed to have applied the approved, in-date methodology and its participant-based impact scale, with deviations listed.

testing.step: Draw a documented sample of scenarios, controls and findings
actions: Take 100% of scenarios scored above tolerance, 100% of Critical and High findings, and 100% of risk acceptances.
Take 12 controls by seeded random selection from those rated effective, weighted to the participant-facing attack paths.
Take 10 findings closed in the period across all severities to test closure quality.
Record the seed, population sizes and selection date so the sample re-draws identically, and confirm the auditor performed no part of the assessment.
testing.done: the sample covers all above-tolerance scenarios, all Critical and High findings, all acceptances and a reproducible selection of effective controls and closures.

testing.step: Re-perform the risk scoring on the sampled scenarios
actions: Take the recorded threat data, asset exposure and incident history for each sampled scenario and re-derive likelihood using the methodology's scale, with the assessor's score hidden.
Re-derive impact from the participant counts and data elements in the frozen inventory and compare to the recorded impact score.
Re-apply the control effectiveness ratings to derive residual risk and compare to the recorded residual.
Confirm every score carries recorded reasoning; an undocumented score is an exception even where the number is defensible.
Confirm the year-on-year movement is explained by a control change rather than a re-scoring judgement, and flag any scenario whose risk fell with no control change.
testing.done: each sampled scenario has independently re-derived likelihood, impact and residual scores compared to the recorded ones, with unexplained year-on-year movement flagged.
